We speculate that social norms about diversity, equity, and inclusion prominent in 2020-21 when these data were collected during the COVID-19 pandemic and shortly after George Floyd’s murder may have heightened faculty’s awareness of gender and race bias, increased motivation to be fair in decision-making, and led to compensatory judgments to increase diversity in STEM careers.

articles.title: Metabolic connectivity
articles.authors: Sharna Jamadar
articles.abstract: The human brain is a complex network, whose functional properties are constrained by its anatomy and energetic constraints. Metabolic connectivity refers to coherent metabolic interactions between spatially distinct regions, and is most commonly measured using [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET). While metabolic connectivity as a field predates fMRI-derived functional connectivity measures, it was not until recently that it was possible to estimate a metabolic network at the individual person level. Here, we review the theoretical and historical contexts of metabolic connectivity, its physiological bases, major methodological approaches, and key findings in health and disease. The review highlights that metabolic connectivity yields unique insight into the functional interactions of the brain relative to fMRI, is predictive of cognition and individual phenotype, and displays unique patterns of time-variant state switching and gradient architecture. We conclude the review with a forward-looking perspective of the future of metabolic connectivity, and recommendations for extending the conceptual framework of the measure.

articles.title: "It's a balancing act": Autistic fathers navigating parenting in everyday life
articles.authors: Chris Edwards; Abigail Love; Ru Ying Cai; Kees-jan Archbald; Dean Dickson; Sean Hynes; Abel Trindade; Sarah Edwards; Bronwyn Leigh; Vicki Gibbs
articles.abstract:
Background
Autistic parents are increasingly recognized as an important source of insight into Autistic adulthood and family life, yet the perspectives of Autistic people who identify as fathers remain almost entirely absent from research. Fathers have distinct experiences, and the absence of their stories and perspectives limits understanding of Autistic parenting more broadly. This study addressed this gap by exploring how Autistic fathers understand and experience parenting across the lifespan.
Methods
We co-produced the study with four Autistic fathers who contributed to design, interview development, and analysis. Nineteen Autistic fathers took part in semi-structured interviews, either spoken or written, depending on their preference. We analyzed the data using reflexive thematic analysis informed by constructionist and participatory research principles.
Results
Our analysis generated five themes: (1) Finding joy and meaning in everyday moments, which captured the emotional rewards of fatherhood; (2) Becoming myself through fatherhood, describing how parenting strengthened self-understanding and Autistic identity; (3) Walking the tightrope of family life, reflecting the effort of balancing sensory, emotional, and practical demands; (4) Parenting as relational work, showing how fathers negotiated understanding and communication within family relationships and the tension that arose when they felt misunderstood; and (5) Parenting in systems stacked against us, highlighting the barriers encountered in services and wider society.
Conclusion
Autistic fathers’ accounts deepen understanding of Autistic adulthood and family life. Their experiences show that fatherhood can strengthen identity and connection while exposing the limits of systems that rarely recognize Autistic needs. These fathers’ insights call for change in how research, policy, and services engage with Autistic people and their families.

articles.title: Promoting well-doing: A Positive Psychology intervention for regulating performance momentum and thriving among high achievers
articles.authors: David Foster; D D Allan
articles.abstract: The present study examined a novel journalling intervention designed to support subjective wellbeing and perceived work performance among high achievers. Sixty-seven university students reporting a grade average of B+ or higher completed a one-week, within-subjects pre–post study involving a daily ‘well done’ journalling task focused on small actions done well. Subjective wellbeing and perceived work performance were measured pre- and post- intervention; with journalling frequency and qualitative feedback collected afterwards. Findings indicated no detectable change in wellbeing from an elevated baseline, however, a significant improvement in perceived work performance was observed. Post-hoc analyses revealed a dose–response pattern, with stronger performance improvements among participants with frequent task engagement. Qualitative feedback was generally favourable, suggesting perceived benefits in positive affect, self-esteem, and motivation. Overall, results show preliminary support for ‘well done’ journalling to enhance perceived performance in high-achieving students.

articles.title: Anxiety modulates sensitivity and response bias in the AX CPT task
articles.authors: Garima Joshi; Bhoomika Rastogi Kar
articles.abstract: Anxiety is associated with altered cognitive control; however, the nature of this alteration may differ across three levels of trait anxiety and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). We examined whether anxiety modulates proactive and reactive control in a context processing task, AX Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT). In Experiment 1a, healthy young adults varying in trait anxiety level were grouped into low, medium, and high trait anxiety categories and completed the AX-CPT. High trait anxious participants showed preserved overall task performance, contextual sensitivity, stronger cue-based expectancy bias and greater susceptibility to probe-level interference than medium and low trait anxious participants. In Experiment 1b, GAD participants were compared with high trait anxious participants on the same task. The GAD participants demonstrated reduced contextual sensitivity, lower cue and probe discriminability, poorer overall performance but a comparable strategic response bias, indicating less precise maintenance and use of contextual information. In turn, this suggests that the effects of high trait anxiety are manifested in the modulation of strategic weighting of predictive cues without affecting the proactive control mechanism, while GAD is associated with a general decrease in the fidelity of context representation. Thus, the anxiety-related differences in cognitive control involve not only quantitative but also qualitative distinct patterns of cue-based preparation and contextual implementation.

articles.title: From backlog to blind spots: why neurodevelopmental pathway reform must start with system mapping
articles.authors: Sima Rafiei; Gemma Cartwright; Ben Atkins; Carla Toro
articles.abstract: Autism and ADHD pathway reform is often framed around waiting lists and capacity. However, backlog data alone cannot show how people move through referral, triage, assessment, support and follow-up, or where inequities and unmet need are hidden. Current data also struggle to distinguish confirmed diagnosis, suspected diagnosis, disclosure, self-identification and co-occurring needs. This creates pathway blindness: systems can see pressure, but not flow, fairness or diagnostic visibility. We argue that reform should begin with structured system mapping, agreed definitions and a realistic minimum dataset before dashboards or predictive analytics are used to guide service change.

articles.title: Distributional latent-variable modeling of ordinal language data
articles.authors: Lukas Sönning; Manfred Krug; Fabian Vetter
articles.abstract: Ordinal response variables are common in linguistic research, particularly in questionnaire and acceptability-judgment studies. They are frequently converted to numeric scores and analyzed using linear (mixed-effects) regression models. This form of analysis is unable to account for scale-induced constraints on the spread of scores. This paper demonstrates how the latent-variable formulation of cumulative-link ordinal regression models can be extended to a distributional (location-scale) framework, enabling the analyst to separately model systematic variation in both the location (central tendency) and scale (spread) of responses. We discuss how scale effects, i.e. systematic variation in the spread of responses, relate to participant- and item-specific response patterns documented in survey research (e.g., extreme, midpoint, and mild response styles) and consider alternatives to the standard z-score transformation used in experimental syntax. Drawing on lexical preference ratings from the Bamberg Survey of Language Variation and Change, we illustrate the approach with data on British–American English synonym pairs rated by Maltese English speakers over a 15-year period. Our case study shows that item-specific scale effects carry genuine linguistic information: Real-time changes in both the location and spread of responses reveal patterns consistent with leader-driven language change, where early adopters drive increased variability before the wider community follows. Bayesian hierarchical models are used for estimation.

articles.title: A single-item signal detection model probes stimulus-specific memorability and its consistency
articles.authors: Igor Utochkin; Keisuke Fukuda
articles.abstract: The concept of memorability has recently become one of the prominent topics in memory research. It highlights that some stimuli are consistently remembered better or cause more false recognition than others across people. We present evidence that items are not equally consistent in producing effects on true and false recognition and show the implications of unequal consistency for measuring and understanding memorability. We applied receiver operating characteristic analysis to a confidence rating recognition-memory task. This allowed us to build an unequal-variance signal-detection (UVSD) “memorability continuum” where each item as memory target or foil produces a populational familiarity distribution characterized by mean and variability. Exploration of the UVSD continuum revealed properties of item-specific representations hidden from traditional analysis of binary “old/new” responses. (1) Although within-item hit and false-alarm rates often show near-zero correlation, taking unequal variability into account revealed a negative correlation between target’s and foil’s mean familiarity, consistent with a recognition-memory “mirror effect”. (2) Foil distributions underlying “false-alarmability” differ considerably in mean and variability, and these parameters are uncorrelated, highlighting variability as an independent aspect of memorability. (3) For targets, variability increased with mean familiarity, suggesting that a stronger memorability boost from encoding is accompanied by greater variation across people. These findings introduce representational variability as a dimension of memorability suggesting that stimuli differ not only in average familiarity but also in the consistency of their mnemonic effects across observers. This establishes a richer approach to studying determinants of memorability and further aligns the field with existing recognition-memory frameworks.

articles.title: The robustness of implicit evaluation updating: Tests of time course and resistance to the return of negativity
articles.authors: Benedek Kurdi; Thomas Cornell Mann; Jordan Axt; Melissa J. Ferguson
articles.abstract: Accumulating evidence suggests that even highly negative implicit (automatic) social evaluations are amenable to temporary shifts toward positivity; however, demonstrations of long-term change, especially in the negative-to-positive direction, are rare. Here we report 10 experiments (9 preregistered; total N = 3,103) probing whether negative-to-positive reversals in implicit evaluations can persist over time and are robust to subsequent negative learning. To this end, we first identified two procedures involving diagnostic behavioral information (reinterpretation and negation + replacement) that, when measured immediately following the intervention, overturned experimentally created implicit negativity toward novel social targets, as measured by the Affect Misattribution Procedure (AMP; Experiments 1–2B). Attesting to the durability of this effect, negative-to-positive reversals persisted without any decrement over a 2-day delay (Experiment 3). Exposure to subsequent negative information on day 3 caused a return of implicit evaluations to negativity, indicating vulnerability to new learning (Experiments 4–5). However, critically, this shift did not reflect unique potentiation of negative learning by initial negative information: The negativity emerging in the positive-to-negative updating condition was statistically equivalent to that following univalent positive initial learning (Experiments 6A–6C) or in the absence of any prior learning (Experiment 7). Demonstrating the flexibility of automatic evaluative processing, these data suggest that negative-to-positive implicit evaluation change can be both durable over time and robust against the potentiation of subsequent negative learning. We discuss implications for social cognitive theory and the prospect of durably changing well-established implicit evaluations of known targets.

articles.title: Normalization of anticipatory neural activity in PTSD after EMDR psychotherapy
articles.authors: Raffaele Costanzo; Biancamaria Di Bello; Maria Gabriela Bevacqua; Francesco Di Russo; Francesca Strappini; Valentina Sulpizio; Sabrina Pitzalis
articles.abstract:
Post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is associated with persistent alterations in cognitive control and decision making, yet the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying psychotherapy related improvement remain incompletely understood. In particular, little is known about how evidence based treatments modulate proactive neural processes supporting anticipation and preparatory control. The present study investigated the clinical, behavioral, and neurophysiological effects of Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) psychotherapy in individuals with PTSD, with a specific focus on pre stimulus neural activity.
Eighteen patients with PTSD and twenty four age  and sex matched healthy controls performed a discriminative response task during electroencephalographic EEG recording at baseline (T0) and follow up (T1). Patients underwent EMDR psychotherapy, whereas controls were reassessed after a comparable time interval. Clinical symptoms, behavioral performance, and pre stimulus event related potential (ERP) components indexing anticipatory motor preparation and proactive cognitive control - namely the Bereitschaftspotential (BP) and the prefrontal Negativity (pN) - were analyzed.
At baseline, patients with PTSD showed greater symptom severity, slower and more variable behavioral responses, higher error rates, and reduced BP and pN amplitudes relative to controls. Following EMDR psychotherapy, patients exhibited significant reductions in anxiety, depressive, and dissociative symptoms, accompanied by faster, more stable, and more accurate task performance. Critically, BP and pN amplitudes increased after treatment, such that post treatment values no longer differed from those of healthy controls. No significant changes were observed in the control group across sessions.
Overall, these findings suggest that EMDR psychotherapy improves clinical symptoms, behavioral functioning, and anticipatory neural processes involved in cognitive control and response preparation in PTSD.

articles.title: Geometric and Topological Predictors of Step-Level Errors in the Corsi Block-Tapping Task
articles.authors: Sergey Malykh; Timofey Adamovich; Victoria Ismatullina; Pavel Kolyasnikov; Artem Malykh
articles.abstract: Conventional scoring of the Corsi block-tapping task reduces each trial to a span or accuracy, discarding where an error falls and the local geometry that may have produced it. We modelled step-level error with a discrete-time hazard model of the probability that a step is incorrect, given that the participant reached it, in a web-based sample (N = 7,132 aged 7–22; 53,031 trials; 221,895 step-level observations) with layout and sequences fixed and identical across participants. Five geometric predictor families—absolute position, relative position, local kinematics, global path complexity, and chunk structure—were each tested against a baseline of step position, age, sex, and sequence length. Because the five are alternative representations of one geometry, we asked whether geometry predicts error and whether those representations differ. All five predicted step-level error beyond the baseline, but the representations were not interchangeable, dissociating by level: stimulus-side families shaped individual steps—error was higher for central and crowded targets—yet washed out at the trial level, whereas trajectory-side families discriminated whole trials, error rising with sharper turns, more overall turning, and larger chunks. Chunk structure carried the largest effect and added reliable step-level information beyond metric path shape, though it all but vanished at the trial level. The geometric contribution was modest but consistent, alongside a steady age-related decline and a small male advantage. The findings are consistent with a Corsi sequence being held in working memory across several scales at once—configural, transitional, and chunked—rather than as a single capacity; on a fixed board these scales operate jointly.

articles.title: Depressive Symptom Trajectories Around the Retirement Transition Across Countries and Historical Periods
articles.authors: Yufei Zhang; Zhihao Ma
articles.abstract: As global aging accelerates, retirement has become a critical transition in older adults’ lives, with profound implications for mental health. Depression trajectories around retirement are inconsistent, with some studies suggesting worsening symptoms and others indicating improvement. Using HRS (United States, 1994–2020), SHARE (Europe and Israel, 2004–2022), CHARLS (China, 2011–2020), and KLoSA (South Korea, 2006–2020), this study examined depressive symptom trajectories around retirement. We emphasized three key components of the retirement transition: retirement age, pre-retirement phase, and post-retirement phase. Using multilevel models, we estimated changes in depressive symptoms around retirement transition, accounting for cross-national and historical differences. Results showed that depressive symptom trajectories varied across datasets and historical periods, but average changes were generally modest. HRS showed pre-retirement increases, an immediate rise at retirement, and post-retirement decline. SHARE showed mainly a small immediate decrease, CHARLS showed a steady increase across the retirement transition, and KLoSA showed an immediate increase followed by post-retirement decline. Period-specific analyses showed further variation, although many trajectories remained close to stable; in CHARLS, later retirement periods showed steeper post-retirement increases. The findings show that retirement-related changes in depressive symptoms are often modest at the group level, while small departures from stability may vary by temporal phase and historical context.

articles.title: Transtheoretical components of evidence-based psychological interventions for stimulant use disorders: a systematically developed taxonomy
articles.authors: Chrysanthi Blithikioti; Camilla Cadorin; Marcella Lucente; Lorena Pizzocri; Giuliano Tomei; Matt Field; Patricia Logullo; Wolfgang Lutz; Toshi A. Furukawa; Ioana Cristea
articles.abstract:
Importance: Psychological interventions are a mainstay of treatment for substance use disorders (SUDs), but their ingredients remain unknown.
Objective: Identify components of evidence-based psychological interventions for a SUD class and develop a transtheoretical taxonomy.
Data sources: The National Library of Medicine via PubMed, searched on 11/01/2023 (update 04/01/2025) for network meta-analyses (NMAs) published since 11/01/2018, using keywords related to substance types, psychotherapy and NMAs.
Study selection: Evidence-based psychological interventions were identified from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) included in one large, recent NMA of stand-alone interventions targeting stimulant use disorders. This NMA comprised 50 RCTs comparing any structured psychosocial intervention to active control or treatment as usual for stimulant (cocaine and/or amphetamine) use disorder in adults, with 10 more RCTs identified in the search update. Two independent researchers identified all intervention arms containing structured psychological components.
Data extraction and synthesis: PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines were followed. Two researchers retrieved complete intervention descriptions (e.g., protocols, manuals) and independently and iteratively extracted components, with multiple consensus meetings for groups of 3-5 RCTs to standardize extraction and coding decisions. Components were organized into higher-order categories with shared functional characteristics and unified definitions. The taxonomy was discussed and amended in a 2.5-days expert meeting. Inter-rater reliability (Cohen’s kappa) was estimated for a random subset of 35% of intervention arms, assessed independently by two new researchers.
Main outcome(s) and measure(s): Transtheoretical components and unique intervention profiles, defined as distinct combinations of these. 
Results: 109 psychological intervention arms yielded 1592 elements, subsequently consolidated into 25 distinct transtheoretical components. Based on this taxonomy, 109 psychological arms were condensed in 40 unique profiles. The most frequently employed components were relapse prevention (34 profiles), functional analysis (32), skill generalization (29), and therapeutic alliance (29). The least frequent components were mindfulness & meditation (3) and subpopulation issues (4). Cohen’s kappa was fair (0.2-0.40) for two components, moderate (0.41-0.6) for four, and substantial (over 0.60) for eleven (remaining components had low prevalence). 
Conclusions and relevance: Recasting psychological interventions as unique combinations of transtheoretical components instead of trademarked protocols could revolutionize treatment evaluation and delivery and accelerate mechanisms of change identification.

articles.title: What Elicits Disgust Across Societies? Evidence from the Ethnographic Record
articles.authors: Roza Gizem Kamiloğlu; Joshua M. Tybur; DANIEL FESSLER
articles.abstract: Disgust is widely viewed as universal, yet most existing research focuses on participants from educated, industrialised large-scale societies. We drew on the Human Relations Area Files to analyse ethnographic descriptions of disgust from 52 societies, which span all eight world regions and every major subsistence type. Grouping free-text descriptions of each disgust elicitor by semantic similarity, without pre-set categories, we identified thirteen recurring themes: bodily wastes and poor hygiene; death, corpses, and tabooed foods; animals; sexual norm violations; incest; political and trust violations; supernatural and ritual transgression; disrespect and harm; property and contract violations; marriage and family strife; hospitality breaches; task and infrastructure failure; and cowardice. The most frequently mentioned elicitors were also those documented in the widest range of societies. Three functional domains proposed by adaptationist perspectives—pathogen, sexual, and moral disgust—were each identifiable across societies, with moral disgust the most widely documented, followed by pathogen disgust and then sexual disgust. Results suggest widespread commonalities in what elicits disgust across societies. We discuss these findings with regard to plausible interactions between biologically evolved psychological mechanisms and cultural evolution.

articles.title: When Importance Isn’t Important: The Paradox in Individually Weighted Models and William James's Perspective
articles.authors: Nicholas Francesco Graziani; Herbert W Marsh; Jiesi Guo; John hattie
articles.abstract:
Individually weighted-average models (IWAMs) assume that domain-specific self-perceptions are weighted by their personal importance when forming global self-evaluations, an assumption derived from William James's (1890) classic formulation of self-worth. Despite its intuitive appeal and continued widespread acceptance, empirical support for this assumed weighting mechanism remains weak and inconsistent. We provide a comprehensive test of whether self-reported importance functions as the psychological weight implied by IWAMs. We compare IWAMs with unweighted and group-weighted models based on aggregated importance ratings and empirically derived regression weights, using a staged design incorporating multitrait–multimethod validation, manifest model comparisons, and fully latent structural equation models.

IWAMs did not outperform empirically derived group-weighted models and provided little evidence that self-perceived importance functions as the psychological weight implied by the Jamesian formulation. Across analytic frameworks, self-concept × importance interactions contributed negligible additional variance. Multiple measures of importance demonstrated acceptable construct validity, including convergent and discriminant validity, core–non-core differences in means, and expected relations with global self-concept, indicating that while importance ratings have construct validity, they do not function as the actual weighting mechanism assumed by the Jamesian model. Instead, although weighting processes are clearly evident, they are not captured by explicit self-reports of importance, providing little support for an idiographic weighting process. Rather, weighting appears to reflect shared weighting structures not captured by importance ratings.

More broadly, these findings challenge the use of subjective self-reports as indicators of weighting mechanisms and highlight the need to distinguish construct validity from mechanism validity when evaluating weighted-average models.

articles.title: Linearity-preserving scores for general measurement errors
articles.authors: Mathias Berggren
articles.abstract: We present a model of how errors-in-variables measurements with a certain expectation structure preserve the linear relationship between the latent error-free variables (Theorem 1). This can be used to define scores for variables to preserve that relationship, and allows a simple relationship between latent and observed explained variances and correlations through the variance that remains in the measurements (Corollary 2), similar to the Spearman (1904) correction for classical errors. The model can be used to model the consequences of a broad set of measurement issues (Proposition 2), such as thresholding, misclassification, missing data, and instrumental variables, through a single overarching analytical model. We also provide a further theorem (Theorem 2) that justifies using this model to estimate latent OLS parameters under various error structures by a 2x2-step Expectation-minimization (Em) algorithm. We illustrate the algorithm through three examples. In Example 1, it is used to estimate parameters in logistic regression, at baseline and with missing data in the outcome. In Example 2, it is used to speed up the estimation of tetrachoric correlations. Example 3 illustrates how population information can be incorporated in the algorithm.

articles.title: The paddle effect as a visual-context bias: Evidence from hierarchical Bayesian psychometric modeling
articles.authors: Wenbo Luo; Yuki Yamada
articles.abstract: In modified video-game Pong tasks, participants judge a moving ball to be slower when using a bigger paddle to block it compared to a smaller one. This paddle effect has traditionally been attributed to action-specific perception. However, Kirsch and Kunde (2018) found that the effect still occurred even without active control of the paddle, and therefore speculated that visual input may be relevant. Based on the original dataset, we applied hierarchical Bayesian psychometric modeling to test this main alternative. We formalized and decomposed the visual-input account into two competing candidate mechanisms: the visual-hit and visual-context hypotheses. Computational evidence strongly supported the latter; its estimated magnitude closely aligns with the original behavioral effect. The present findings suggest that the paddle effect acts as a visual-context bias.

articles.title: Bias and accuracy of effect size estimation in sequential Bayes factor designs
articles.authors: Wenbo Luo; Yuki Yamada
articles.abstract: The sequential Bayes factor (SBF) design improves sampling efficiency by allowing for optional stopping, but its impact on overall estimation quality remains insufficiently characterized. In this simulation study, we evaluated estimation bias and accuracy across a full-factorial design incorporating four true effect sizes and three distributional skewness levels. Adopting a dual-metric approach, we quantified estimation performance using bias and root mean square error (RMSE) for both sample-based frequentist and Bayesian posterior estimates. For non-zero effects, sample-based estimates showed systematic overestimation of the true effect sizes. While Bayesian posterior estimation attenuated the directional bias, estimation accuracy remained compromised. Distributional skewness did not qualitatively change this core pattern, confirming that the primary source of estimation distortion is optional stopping itself. We argue that, relative to systematic bias, the loss of estimation accuracy represents a more critical, yet largely underexamined, challenge. By quantifying overall estimation quality beyond bias alone, the present study highlights a critical consideration for researchers adopting SBF designs.

articles.title: Following the Tune: Divergent Processing Strategies for Auditory Sequence Recognition in Humans and a Songbird
articles.authors: Zhi-Yuan Ning; Jiaxin Li; Carel ten Cate; Henkjan Honing
articles.abstract:
Deriving sequential information from complex sounds is a challenge for auditory systems, yet it remains 9
unclear whether humans and nonhuman species integrate concurrent cues or prioritize a single dimension 10
when processing multidimensional input. We investigated shared constraints and species-specific 11
predispositions in processing strategies across humans and zebra finches using an identical operant 12
conditioning paradigm with complex-tone sequences. By presenting probe stimuli that selectively 13
preserved or disrupted either pitch or formant trajectory, we quantified these strategies. We show that 14
zebra finches employ an additive integration strategy, treating pitch and formant trajectories as 15
complementary components of a unified auditory pattern. In contrast, humans exhibit a dominant reliance 16
on pitch. Critically, experience further modulated this bias, revealing cross-dimensional abstraction: 17
trained listeners recruited secondary cues to preserve learned relational structure when pitch was 18
unreliable. These findings imply a cross-species divergence in auditory representation, suggesting that 19
human auditory processing is shaped by an interplay of species-specific priorities and experience- 20
dependent functional substitution.

articles.title: Forbidden Causes: Science as a Restrictive Cognitive System
articles.authors: Ze Hong
articles.abstract: Most of what people in modern societies believe about the world is acquired through deference to scientific institutions rather than through independent verification. This paper asks what such institutions transmit to the lay public beyond particular findings, and argues that they instill a restrictive sense of what kinds of things can exist and what kinds of explanation can be taken seriously. I specify this restrictive sense as four admissibility constraints that narrow the range of candidate explanations before any evidence is considered: explanations should be impersonal, physically mediated, nomologically uniform, and sparsely connected. Rather than identifying which explanations are false, these constraints filter out whole classes of explanation in advance, marking them as the wrong kind of thing to be true. They are most fully entrenched among the scientifically acculturated and operate more unevenly in the general population. I show that the constraints are historically contingent rather than essential to science, since early modern inquiry was considerably more permissive about what might exist. I illustrate their operation through the reception of Newtonian gravitation and the rhetoric of contemporary pseudoscience, and draw out the implications for science education.

articles.title: From Retreat to Reality: A Qualitative Study of How Adolescents Apply Mindfulness One Month After a Weeklong Retreat
articles.authors: Jiaxiong Li; Brian Galla; Michael James Tumminia
articles.abstract:
Objectives 
Mindfulness programs are increasingly delivered to adolescents to help them navigate emotional and social challenges, yet little is known about how they apply these skills after program completion. While most research has focused on short-term, school-based programs and intra-personal outcomes, this qualitative study explored how adolescents integrated mindfulness into their lives one month after participating in an intensive, weeklong retreat. 
Methods
Fifteen adolescents (Mage = 16.74 years, SD = 1.58 years; 73% girls, 27% boys; 53.3% White, 6.7% African American, 6.7% East Asian, and 33.3% Multiracial) completed interviews one month after a six-day mindfulness retreat. Participants reflected on retreat takeaways and described how they applied mindfulness to personal and social challenges. Data were analyzed using a three-cycle coding process to identify patterns in intra- and inter-personal applications.
Results	
Adolescents described intra-personal applications, such as self-awareness and regulation (100% of adolescents; e.g., regulating thoughts and emotions), practicing self-compassion and acceptance (73%; e.g., being less self-critical), and gaining a broader perspective (60%; e.g., focusing on what matters). They also reported inter-personal applications, including navigating social anxiety and building connections (73%; e.g., using mindfulness to reduce social apprehension), engaging in compassionate communication (67%; e.g., active listening and providing emotional support), and greater social awareness and attunement (53%; e.g., practicing empathy and perspective-taking). All adolescents described experiences in both domains.
Conclusions
This study offers insights into how adolescents integrate mindfulness into daily life after an immersive retreat and suggests such experiences foster transferable skills supporting developmental needs. Implications for contemplative science are discussed.

articles.title: Profiling the Chinese Participants in Psychological Science: Non-WEIRD but Not Representative
articles.authors: Lei Yue; Zhangweiwei; Chunxiao Wang; Xi-Nian Zuo; Hu Chuan-Peng
articles.abstract: Psychological science aims at understanding the human mind and behavior, but it primarily relies on participants from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic regions, i.e., the WEIRD problem. This lack of diversity and representativeness of participants compromises the generalizability of psychological science. To address this issue, large-scale international collaborative projects have been initiated, and more data have been collected from non-WEIRD regions. However, it is unknown whether participants from non-WEIRD regions can represent their local population. In this preregistered report, we depicted the demographic profile of Chinese participants reported in 1, 000 empirical studies (n = 554, 794) published in five mainstream Chinese psychological journals and in 27 large-scale international collaborative projects (n = 29, 006, accounting for 2.12% of all participants). We found that age and sex were the most reported demographic variables, and other aspects of participants were less reported. The available demographic information revealed that Chinese participants were not representative of the population: most were young, well-educated, and resided in East China. Also, Chinese participants in large-scale international collaborative projects are less representative than those from Chinese journals in terms of geographical distributions. The demographic profile of Chinese participants in psychology is similar to their counterparts in many other countries and regions, suggesting the globalization of young and highly educated participants in psychological science. Together, our findings indicate that problems of representativeness are deeply entrenched in global psychological science and require coordinated cross-sector efforts.

articles.title: On Why Meta-d′ May Not Go the Distance: Confidence Distance as a Calibration-Based Measure of Metacognition
articles.authors: Domenic Groh
articles.abstract: Meta-d' is widely used to quantify metacognitive sensitivity, and the meta-d'/d' ratio is commonly interpreted as metacognitive efficiency. However, both depend on assumptions inherited from signal detection theory, including Gaussian evidence distributions and a shared latent evidence axis for type-1 decisions and confidence judgments. These assumptions are not guaranteed in many behavioral paradigms. The present paper examines how violations of these assumptions affect meta-d' and the meta-d'/d' ratio, and introduces Confidence Distance as a calibration-based measure of metacognitive performance. Confidence Distance is defined as the mean absolute distance between trial-wise confidence and objective correctness after mapping confidence ratings onto the unit interval. Across simulation studies, non-Gaussian evidence distributions distorted the meta-d'/d' ratio even when metacognitive monitoring was ideal. These distortions were not limited to underestimation: heavy-tailed and light-tailed evidence inflated the ratio, whereas skewed evidence reduced it. In addition, when confidence was based on evidence not used for the type-1 response, meta-d' itself became inflated despite unchanged metacognitive ability. Confidence Distance, by contrast, remained comparatively stable across distributional forms, increased monotonically when metacognitive noise was added, and remained well-defined across multidimensional and multi-alternative task structures because it requires only trial-wise correctness and confidence. These findings suggest that meta-d' and the meta-d'/d' ratio conflate metacognitive performance with distributional misspecification or evidence-axis mismatch in applied research contexts. Confidence Distance therefore offers a transparent and assumption-light index of confidence–accuracy correspondence.

articles.title: Coordinated Psychological Intervention Ensembles Outperform Single-Mechanism Designs Across Societal Challenges
articles.authors: Anandita Sabherwal; Danielle Goldwert; Madalina Vlasceanu; Elke U. Weber
articles.abstract: Behavioral science tends to seek the single most predictive explanation for behavioral phenomena and subsequently the most effective intervention for behavior change. Yet many consequential outcomes, from climate action to democratic attitudes, result from multiple psychological processes, raising the question of whether combining interventions that leverage different processes would prove more effective. Across a 13-intervention megastudy and a second, megastudy-informed experiment (Ns = 8,488 and 2,547 US adults; both quota-matched and preregistered) we test whether intervention ensembles—deliberate combinations of distinct psychological modules delivered together—can more effectively shape target behaviors and attitudes.  We test three principles for constructing such ensembles: 1) outcome optimizing ensembles (combining top-performing individual interventions), 2) mechanism coverage ensembles (covering key psychological drivers of the outcome), and 3) multi-level synergy ensembles (combining individual-, collective-, and system-level processes). Ensembles consistently outperformed their constituent single-mechanism interventions. In Study 1, relative to an informed control, the strongest ensemble increased climate policy support by 41.5% and donation by 43.0%. And in Study 2, the ensemble was significantly more effective than its components in reducing partisan animosity and strengthening democratic attitudes. The largest gains were achieved by multi-level synergistic ensembles that aligned processes across individual, collective, and systemic levels. LLM-assisted analyses of participant reasoning reveal that effective ensembles work by resolving complementary psychological barriers, not by simply providing more arguments. For complex societal challenges shaped by multiple barriers, interventions can achieve behavior change at greater rate and scale by designing coordinated intervention ensembles rather than by searching for the single best mechanism.

articles.title: Evidence for the simultaneous sensorimotor representation of observed and imagined actions
articles.authors: Matthew Scott; David Wright; Nicola Jane Hodges; Justine Magnuson; Sarah N Kraeutner
articles.abstract: The human sensorimotor system can represent actions in the absence of movement, termed motor simulation. These motor simulations can be perceptually (externally) driven through observation of an actor or cognitively (internally) driven through imagining movement. Although there is evidence humans can represent multiple actions simultaneously, whether different motor simulations can concurrently be represented is unclear. We investigated the capacity of the sensorimotor system to simultaneously represent observed (action observation; AO) and imagined actions (motor imagery; MI). Two competing hypotheses were tested concerning whether AO and MI could co-exist or not, The Dual Action Simulation Hypothesis (DASH) and Visual Guidance Hypothesis (VGH), respectively. Fifteen participants completed a functional magnetic resonance imagining (fMRI) study, requiring them to complete four distinct conditions involving imagination or observation of a rhythmical hand tapping action. Conditions involved; AO, AO with a counting task (i.e., with cognitive load), MI, or simultaneous AO and MI of different actions (AOMI). Through representational similarity analysis, AO and MI motor simulations were evidenced within the ventral premotor cortex and to an extent the inferior parietal lobule, supporting DASH over VGH. Multidimensional scaling of representational similarity data indicated a unique representational pattern for AOMI, differing with AO and MI across different dimensions. Whole-brain analyses revealed greater engagement of sensorimotor regions during AOMI than the summation of the independent AO and MI conditions. While dual motor simulations appear possible, our data suggests the representational pattern of AOMI is distinct and produces super-additive sensorimotor activity, of which DASH and VGH do not account for.

articles.title: Musical Groove as Stabilization of Coordinated Movement: A Dynamical and Embodied Approach to Musical Rhythm
articles.authors: Ji Chul Kim
articles.abstract: Research showed that the bodily experience of pleasurable urge to move to music, called groove, is the strongest for rhythms with an intermediate level of syncopation. Current theories explain groove in terms of predictive processes in the brain, as an active inference which resolves prediction errors caused by syncopation. Here we present an alternative explanation of groove from a new dynamical and embodied approach to music perception and action. The new theory, called embodied dynamics of music (EDM), describes musical rhythm as a dynamic pattern of coordinated movement distributed in the brain and the body and governed by the principles and constraints of coordination dynamics. Specifically, beat-based rhythm is described as a coordinative structure in which beat-carrying oscillatory movements provide anchor points for coordinating discrete movements corresponding to individual rhythmic events. In this view, syncopation is a potentially destabilizing force in the coordinative structure, and groove is an active engagement that stabilizes the coordinative structure by reinforcing beat-carrying oscillation with body movement. We support this theory with an analysis of coordination dynamics and a minimal dynamical model of groove which stabilizes syncopated coordination with a metronome by amplifying its self-sustained oscillation.

articles.title: From Debate to Practice: Why Research Needs Principle-Driven Frameworks for Responsible AI Use
articles.authors: Florian Buehler
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded across academic research, from writing and translation to literature support, coding, analysis, and image generation. Although the issue is cross-disciplinary, the argument is especially relevant to psychological and behavioral research, where GenAI is increasingly used not only for manuscript preparation but also for literature work, coding, analysis, translation, and research materials. While editorial policies increasingly require disclosure and human accountability, this research commentary argues that policy statements alone are insufficient to produce responsible practice. The current debate unfolds in a climate where suspected AI use may be interpreted as incompetence, laziness, or misconduct, making disclosure socially and reputationally costly. This dynamic is further complicated by uneven enforcement, including the risk that AI-detection tools disproportionately misclassify non-native English writing. The article therefore shifts the question from whether AI use should be disclosed to how disclosure can become practically possible, proportionate, and fair. It distinguishes reporting checklists, which document AI use once it becomes methodologically relevant, from principle-driven frameworks, which help researchers evaluate AI use before submission. Building on recent responsible-AI frameworks, the article argues for tool-agnostic principles that support data security, quality control, originality, transparency, accountability, and broader impact. It concludes that trustworthy AI governance in research requires usable routines, disclosure templates, and proportional editorial evaluation rather than a culture organized primarily around suspicion and exposure.

articles.title: Revisiting the SciPop Scale: Measurement Alignment, Scoring Rules, and Cross-Context Comparability
articles.authors: Xue-Fei Yan; Zhihao Ma
articles.abstract: Science-related populism—populist attitudes toward scientific authority—has attracted growing scholarly attention. Although the SciPop Scale measures this construct, its cross-national psychometric properties remain underexamined. Using data from the Trust in Science and Science-Related Populism project (N = 69,341; 68 countries/regions) and the Swiss Science Barometer (N = 1,124), we evaluate factor structure and reliability, test multigroup invariance, apply alignment for approximate invariance, and compare scoring philosophies (Bollen vs. Goertz approach) on criterion validity. We further employ multidimensional item response theory models to provide complementary item-level diagnostics, including discrimination, threshold, item information, and differential item functioning. Results show that reliability is high and a four-factor model fits most broadly. Full measurement invariance holds across sex, age, education, residence, political orientation, and religiosity; partial invariance appears across regions, economic development, cultural values, and regime types. Cross-national comparability is limited but improves via measurement alignment. Different scoring methods identify different weakest dimensions. For criterion validity, Bollen-based aligned scores consistently outperform Goertz approach, yielding higher explanatory power in cross-national and cross-group analyses. Finally, we provide guidelines for researchers using the SciPop Scale and future directions for measuring science-related populism.

articles.title: Transdiagnostic Physiological Correlates of Unpredictable Threat Anticipation
articles.authors: Hannes Per Carsten; Kai Härpfer; Franziska Magdalena Kausche; Anja Riesel
articles.abstract: Responses to unpredictable threat have been proposed as a candidate mechanism in anxiety-related psychopathology, but clinical findings remain heterogeneous and often rely on single physiological outcomes. The present study examined whether physiological responses during threat anticipation map onto categorical and dimensional conceptualizations of psychopathology across the anxiety and obsessive-compulsive spectrum. In a transdiagnostic sample of N = 163 participants, patients with specific phobia, social anxiety disorder (SAD), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), as well as unaffected controls completed the NPU-threat test in order to measure responses to predictable and unpredictable threat. Physiological responding was assessed using startle reflex, skin conductance responses (SCR), and event-related potentials indexing early sensory processing (N1) and later attentional allocation (P3). Results indicated a group-based effect for SCR, such that patients with OCD showed enhanced autonomic responding during unpredictable threat anticipation. Dimensionally, anxious arousal was associated with reduced SCR during unpredictable threat and lower P3 amplitudes across conditions. Intolerance of uncertainty modulated startle particularly in controls, and anxious apprehension was associated with increased N1 amplitudes in OCD. Exploratory latent profile analysis identified three multisystem physiological response profiles. A threat-reactive profile characterized by increased N1 and both increased SCR and startle to unpredictable threat was particularly clinically enriched, showing higher clinical severity, greater representation of SAD and OCD, and elevated anxious apprehension and social anxiety symptoms. Together, findings suggest that threat anticipation in anxiety-related psychopathology is best understood as a multisystem and partly transdiagnostic process rather than as a single physiological marker of diagnostic status or unpredictable-threat sensitivity.

articles.title: Entrepreneurial Resilience, Costly Signals and Innovative Behavior in Crisis: A Behavioral Ecology Perspective
articles.authors: Georgios Afxentiou
articles.abstract:
The role of psychological resources in entrepreneurial resilience has been extensively discussed and empirically analyzed in many studies. However, an interdisciplinary approach to how resilience enables entrepreneurs to generate costly signals of innovative behavior was not introduced in a scholarly conversation. This complex and challenging exploration on multiple disciplines, drawn from the entrepreneurial resilience and costly signaling theories and integrating insights from behavioral ecology, offers a new perspective on innovative behavior under adverse conditions. A theory synthesis and a cross-disciplinary approach were adopted to analyze the insights from entrepreneurial psychology, resilience research, behavioral ecology, and innovation. A novel conceptual framework and propositions on stress responses, anxiety, and entrepreneurial resilience describe how entrepreneurs could generate costly signals of innovative behavior. This exploratory study proposes that entrepreneurs experiencing anxiety or stress are more likely to generate low-cost signaling, resulting in less credible signals of innovation, which may reduce consumer confidence in their products and services. It provides insights for both scholars and practitioners, offering a foundation for developing strategies that strengthen resilience and foster innovation in crisis contexts.

Keywords: Entrepreneurial resilience, psychological resources, costly signaling, behavioral ecology, innovation, crisis.

articles.title: Neural discrimination of objects, faces, and print in dyslexic and typical readers: A steady-state visual evoked potential study
articles.authors: Irina Ovchinnikova; Hélène Devillez; Heida Maria Sigurdardottir
articles.abstract: Visual processing difficulties have been reported in dyslexia, yet it remains unclear whether dyslexic and typical readers differ in how the visual system rapidly and automatically discriminates between stimuli. In this preregistered study, 31 matched pairs of adult dyslexic and typical readers completed three fast periodic visual stimulation paradigms while we recorded steady-state visual evoked potentials with EEG. Streams of objects, faces, and print were presented at 6 Hz, with every fifth image involving an identity change at 1.2 Hz. Against our predictions, responses to such changes were not lower for the dyslexic group in any paradigm. For objects, dyslexic readers instead showed higher responses to within-category changes despite similar behavioral accuracy, suggesting that greater neural resources were recruited for the same task. Across all three categories, dyslexic readers also showed elevated responses to the rapid image stream, pointing to a general difference in visual encoding. Neural responses to face identity changes predicted recognition accuracy in typical but not dyslexic readers, consistent with the two groups relying on different mechanisms to support behavior. These findings suggest that even in cases where visual discrimination ability is largely intact in adult dyslexic readers, the neural processes that support it and its link to behavior differ from those of typical readers.

articles.title: The ideological differences in institutional trust and conspiratorial mentality across 42 nations
articles.authors: Evan A. Valdes; Matt N Williams
articles.abstract: Public trust in core institutions is often linked to conspiratorial mentality, but this relationship may vary by institutional domain, ideological position, and national context. Using survey data from 24,009 respondents across 42 countries (2018–2019), we estimated multilevel models testing whether trust in political, knowledge-generating, and law-and-order institutions predicted general conspiratorial mentality, whether these associations varied linearly across ideological positions, and whether they showed curvilinear patterns reflecting ideological distance from the center. Political and law-and-order institutional trust were robust negative predictors of conspiratorial mentality across societies, whereas knowledge-generating trust was largely unrelated to conspiratorial mentality on average. Ideology moderated the trust–conspiracy association for political and law-and-order trust: higher trust predicted lower conspiratorial mentality across the ideological spectrum, but this association was weaker among more left-leaning respondents. Quadratic analyses further indicated that conspiratorial mentality was higher farther from the ideological center, with political and law-and-order trust moderating this curvilinear pattern. Country-specific estimates showed that these associations varied across societies. These findings suggest that the relationship between trust and conspiratorial mentality varies across institutional domains, ideological position, and national context, consistent with motivated reasoning accounts in which trust is interpreted through identity-relevant legitimacy cues.

articles.title: Format-invariant semantic dimensions structure food similarity judgments
articles.authors: Jason Avery; Charles Zheng; Caroline Candy; Andrew Persichetti; Alex Martin
articles.abstract: Our knowledge about food integrates sensory, affective, functional, and cultural information that is not reducible to visual appearance or nutritional composition. We asked whether human food similarity judgments are organized by semantic dimensions that generalize across presentation format. Participants completed large-scale odd-one-out triplet tasks for the same 68 foods presented either as photographs or written names, fully sampling all possible triplets in each modality. We fit VICE, a sparse Bayesian embedding model, independently to image and word judgments, then identified stable dimensions matched across modalities. This procedure revealed nine format-invariant consensus dimensions. These consensus dimensions accounted for nearly all predictable triplet behavior, outperforming models based on explicit food property ratings, objective macronutrients, low-level image statistics, and general object-property embeddings. The dimensions showed interpretable relationships with subjective food properties and, to a lesser extent, nutritional content, and showed partial overlap with the broader THINGS object-property space. Out-of-sample validation showed that the same dimensions generalized to independent food similarity datasets. Finally, analyses of dimension contributions across triplet judgments indicated that food similarity is not well described as a strictly two-dimensional space or a simple hierarchy. Instead, a small number of broad dimensions that capture coarse distinctions among food types coexist with finer-grained dimensions that discriminate both within and across those divisions. These findings suggest that food knowledge is organized by a multidimensional semantic structure that is stable across format, partly shared with general object cognition, and enriched by food-specific distinctions.

articles.title: Is physical activity associated with lower borderline personality disorder severity, accounting for insomnia disorder?
articles.authors: Valentin Krieger; Samuel St-Amour; Paquito Bernard; Niharika Parashar; Matthieu Samson; Lionel Cailhol
articles.abstract:
Background:
Borderline personality disorder is associated with severe suffering and insomnia. Physical activity has been related to improvements in borderline personality disorder and sleep disorders. However, no study has yet analyzed the relationship between physical activity and borderline personality disorder, accounting for insomnia disorder. This study aimed to fill this gap in the literature. 
Method:
This cross-sectional study recruited 192 participants aged 18 years and over reporting a borderline personality disorder. Participants had to fill out an online survey collecting information about their mental health, sleep disorders, and physical activity habits. An analysis of covariance was computed with R.
Results:
The overall model explained a significant amount of variance in borderline personality disorder (R² = .19, p < .001). Being physically active was not significantly associated with lower borderline personality disorder after controlling for insomnia disorder (F(1,189) = 1.18, p = .28). Insomnia disorder was strongly and significantly associated with borderline personality disorder (F(1,189) = 46.15, p < .001).
Conclusion:
The findings suggest that insomnia disorder is a particularly relevant correlate of borderline personality disorder, whereas physical activity appears less central. Clinically, this highlights the importance of assessing sleep-related problems. Future research should examine these associations using experimental and longitudinal designs.

articles.title: The Dynamic Contingency Model: Integrating competing theories of personality processes
articles.authors: Muchen Xi; Joshua James Jackson
articles.abstract: Despite decades of theoretical development proposing how personality traits, situational contingencies, and person-environment transactions jointly govern behavioral variability, there lacks a direct comparison these competing accounts within a unified empirical framework. The present study addresses this gap by introducing the Dynamic Contingency Model (DCM), a framework based on Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling that simultaneously captures within-person person-environment temporal dynamics, situation-behavior contingencies, and stable between-person differences. Using intensive longitudinal data from 306 undergraduates across 25 personality-situation combinations, we pursued three major aims: (1) identifying the most plausible theoretical model of daily behavioral dynamics; (2) identifying the effective pathways in person-environment transactions; and (3) examining individual differences and trait moderation in dynamic processes. The DCM consistently outperformed all competing models, including static trait, situational contingency models, person-situation interaction models, and traditional transaction models. Within the DCM, autoregressive effects and contemporaneous situation contingencies emerged as the dominant parameters, with cross-lagged transactions exhibiting a systematic asymmetry whereby personality states more robustly predicted subsequent situational experiences than vice versa, suggesting individuals function as active architects of their daily dynamics. Substantial individual differences in dynamic parameters were observed, yet Big Five traits explained only a modest fraction of this variability. Together, these findings establish that personality dynamics are best characterized as a multifaceted system integrating dispositional, situational, and temporal processes.

articles.title: Tonic Pupil-Linked Arousal Modulates Global Response Efficiency but Not Spatial Orienting
articles.authors: Ana-Maria Barosan; Simon van Gaal; Shriya Kashyap; Jakub Jurák; Timo Stein
articles.abstract: Arousal fluctuations shape behavioural performance, with optimal performance often observed at intermediate arousal levels, but it remains unclear whether these effects primarily arise during stimulus encoding, attentional orienting, decision formation, or motor execution. Here, we asked whether arousal modulates spatial orienting specifically, or instead affects broader components of task performance. Across four exogenous and one endogenous Posner cueing experiments, we tested whether spontaneous fluctuations in tonic arousal, indexed by pre-stimulus pupil size, modulate spatial orienting. Overall response speed followed a robust U-shaped relationship with pupil-linked arousal: responses were fastest at intermediate pupil sizes and slower at both smaller and larger pupil sizes. In contrast, spatial cueing effects were not consistently modulated by pupil-linked arousal. Together, these findings reveal a dissociation between arousal-related changes in response speed and spatial orienting. More broadly, these results suggest that tonic arousal can modulate task performance without necessarily altering selective attention.

articles.title: Sentence comprehension with syntax–plausibility conflict under articulatory suppression: An fMRI study
articles.authors: Rei Emura; Hyeonjeong Jeong; Yousuke Kawachi; Ryuya Komuro; Masatoshi Koizumi
articles.abstract: Introduction: Human sentence comprehension relies on limited cognitive resources that support both syntactic processing and the integration of world knowledge. Previous neuroimaging studies have investigated how working memory, particularly the phonological loop, supports the processing of syntactically complex sentences. However, less is known about whether phonological-loop constraints modulate neural responses to conflicts between syntactic structure and plausibility based on world knowledge. Methods: Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, this study investigates comprehension accuracy and brain activity during comprehension of plausible and implausible Japanese sentences under a single-task condition and a dual-task condition involving concurrent articulation. Results: Whole-brain analyses revealed lower comprehension accuracy and greater activation in regions including the bilateral inferior frontal gyrus and the supplementary motor area for implausible than for plausible sentences. However, no significant interaction between plausibility and secondary task was found, suggesting that the plausibility effect was observed regardless of whether participants performed concurrent articulation. At the same time, region-of-interest (ROI) analyses further showed that both the left inferior frontal gyrus pars triangularis (LIFGtri) and pars orbitalis (LIFGorb) were sensitive to plausibility, whereas only LIFGtri was modulated by task demands. Discussion: These findings suggest that syntax--plausibility conflict remains behaviorally and neurally detectable under articulatory suppression. It is consistent with the view that the phonological loop plays a limited role in sentence comprehension, primarily maintaining incoming linguistic information rather than supporting the integration of syntactic structure with world knowledge. The ROI results further suggest the possibility of functional differences within the LIFG: LIFGtri may be more sensitive to overall task demands, whereas LIFGorb may support relatively stable sentence-level interpretation.

articles.title: A field guide to causal inference and sensitivity analysis methods for science education researchers
articles.authors: Huibin Zhang; Joshua Rosenberg; Ken Frank; Wei Wang; Ran Xu
articles.abstract: Many of us in science education understand experimental design, but the broader world of causal inferences is known and established.. Complicating this is how causal inference methods and related techniques—namely robustness analyses and sensitivity analyses—all fit together, and why researchers might use one or an assemblage of these methods. Our aims are to a) disambiguate between the broad collection of causal inference methods and sensitivity analyses, b) provide guidance for when and how to choose among causal inference techniques, and c) explain when and how sensitivity analyses are appropriate to use alongside other techniques. To achieve these aims, we provide four worked examples (i.e., propensity score analysis, regression discontinuity, differences in difference, and instrumental variables) grounded in science education contexts (either through datasets or simulations),, and by illustrating how sensitivity analysis can be used alongside each causal inference method to assess robustness. The overarching contribution of this paper is a kind of “field guide” for science education researchers interested in making stronger claims about statistical effects.

articles.title: The social transmission of linguistic alignment: the role of observational reinforcement learning
articles.authors: Yichi ZHANG; Zhenguang Garry Cai
articles.abstract: People align their linguistic use in conversations and it has been proposed that such linguistic alignment facilitates mutual understanding and social rapport. However, the mechanisms through which perspective alignment is socially transmitted across individuals remain unclear. Here, we combined behavioral experiments and computational learning models to investigate whether, and if so, how observing aligned and non-aligned responses in others affects the perspective alignment of observers. Participants completed a three-phase design: they first played a referential game with a child interlocutor (baseline), then completed an observation phase in which, on each trial, they watched an adult demonstrator, who exhibited either high or low alignment with the child’s referential perspective and predicted the demonstrators choice before observing it, and then played a round with the child themselves (observation), and finally played with a new child (generalization). Observing high alignment increased observers’ own alignment, whereas observing low alignment decreased it, and these changes carried over to the new child, indicating a transferable communicative strategy rather than a partner-specific adjustment. To identify the underlying mechanism, we modelled behaviour trial by trial. A Rescorla–Wagner model first confirmed that participants learned to predict the demonstrator’s choices. We then used Bayesian model comparison to adjudicate three accounts of how alignment changed. A model driven by observational prediction errors (i.e., the discrepancy between participants’ predictions and the demonstrator’s actual choices) outperformed both an imitation account (copying the most recent choice) and a priming account (the cumulative frequency of the demonstrator’s aligned responses). In the high alignment group, both positive and negative prediction errors in the second half of the observation phase predicted alignment changes, whereas in the low alignment group, negative prediction errors predicted decreased alignment. Exploratory analyses further suggested that alignment may function as a social signal: observers rated high-alignment demonstrators as more perspective-taking than low-alignment demonstrators. Together, these findings show that perspective alignment can be socially transmitted through prediction-error-driven observational learning, neither passive copying nor mere exposure, and offer a computational account of how communicative strategies spread across individuals.

articles.title: Supporting Children on Therapy Waitlists: A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Web-Based Parent-Focused Single Session Intervention for Child Anxiety
articles.authors: Madelaine Abel; Jessica L. Schleider; Jenna Yejin Sung; Alayna D'Amico; Dina R. Hirshfeld-Becker
articles.abstract: Many children experience significant, impairing anxiety, yet most never access evidence-based support; among those who do, most face long wait-times to be seen. This disconnect reflects a need for intervention approaches that provide rapid access to interim care. Single-session interventions (SSIs) may help mitigate the adverse impacts of long waitlists. This pilot parallel group RCT evaluated the effectiveness and acceptability of a self-guided, web-based SSI delivered to parents of children ages 4-13 (Mage=8.84) with anxiety or OCD on a waitlist at a hospital-based Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy (CBT) clinic. The SSI, Project EMPOWER, targets parental accommodation, a family factor that can worsen child anxiety and impede efficacy of CBT. Parents were randomized to receive the SSI (N=24) or waitlist as usual (N=23). Parents completed a baseline diagnostic interview about their child and self-report questionnaires about their accommodation of child anxiety, child anxiety symptoms, and perceived ability to manage their child’s anxiety (parent agency) at baseline, 2-week follow-up, and CBT intake. Relative to controls, parents who received the SSI reported significant reductions in their accommodation (d=0.59, p=.046) and child anxiety (d=1.25, p<.001) and significant increases in parent agency (d=0.68, p=.02) from baseline to 2-week follow-up. Effects were maintained until children started CBT (mean time =13.54 weeks). Additionally, parents rated the SSI as highly acceptable in accordance with preregistered benchmarks. Results support the effectiveness and acceptability of a web-based, self-guided SSI for parents of children on therapy waitlists, offering a scalable approach to support families while they wait for formal treatment.

articles.title: Reduced Visual Imagery Vividness as a Risk Factor for PTSD: Implications for Aphantasia and Imagery-Based Treatments
articles.authors: Diane Swick; Sandy Lwi; Jary Larsen
articles.abstract: Recent theoretical models such as the generative adversarial framework propose that the ability to generate high-fidelity visual images may intensify the severity of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), particularly the intrusive re-experiencing of traumatic events. Meanwhile, individuals with minimal imagery (aphantasia) may be protected. To evaluate this relationship, 312 Veterans completed the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) and the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5). Results indicated that lower VVIQ scores (less vivid imagery) were associated with greater PTSD severity. This inverse relationship was observed across all PTSD symptom clusters, with the strongest association for the negative cognition/mood cluster. Five of the eight Veterans who reported very low VVIQ scores (consistent with aphantasia) had clinically significant PTSD and high levels of intrusive symptoms, further indicating that aphantasia was not protective. These findings have implications for PTSD treatments and suggest that reduced visual imagery is associated with impaired processing of traumatic experiences.

articles.title: Indigenous Perspectives of Trauma-Sensitive Yoga Using Community-Based and Consensual Qualitative Frameworks
articles.authors: Kelsey Madison Dietrich; Linda Zheng; Ashley Baumann; Jill Kessler; Lyndsey Ducheneaux; Viann N Nguyen-Feng
articles.abstract:
Objective: Indigenous communities endure intergenerational and ongoing traumas. Trauma Center Trauma-Sensitive Yoga (TCTSY) is an empirically-supported yoga-based intervention for complex trauma. To become a TCTSY-Facilitator, candidates complete a 20-hour training followed by a 300-hour certification program. This community-based research documented the first Indigenous TCTSY-Facilitator Training Cohort’s perspectives on TCTSY’s acceptability, feasibility, and utility. 
Method: Protocols were developed with community partners, and researchers engaged in reflexivity practices and Indigenous cultural learnings. Twenty interviews were conducted with 15 adult interviewees: 14 program participants (13 women) who completed the 20-hour training and 1 program mentor. From the 14 program participants (11 Great Plains Tribal Nations, with 4 Tribal citizens and 7 descendents), 10 enrolled in the 300-hour training, and 3 completed the full certification. Interviews were analyzed using the consensual qualitative research method. 
Results: Most participants reported the training positively impacted their approach to trauma care and some aspects (e.g., body-based modality) aligned with current healing approaches. Common training takeaways included learning about the effects of trauma and the value of invitational language. Participants endorsed intentions to integrate TCTSY for personal and community healing; examples of integration included smudging/burning of medicines (e.g., sage), land-based practice for connection to nature, and intentional movement within ceremony space. Program improvements included additional emphasis on yoga history/philosophy, collaborations with Elders, and acknowledgment of current community trauma. 
Conclusion: A community-based research framework provided opportunities to explore the feasibility, acceptability, and utility of TCTSY for Indigenous communities in a culturally-relevant and trauma-informed way.

articles.title: Voice as a Cognitive Anchor: The VOCES Framework for Identity Preservation in Early Cognitive Decline
articles.authors: Lisette Diaz-Santiago
articles.abstract: As global populations age, early cognitive decline increasingly affects individuals and the families navigating identity disruption and relational strain alongside them. Contemporary memory-support interventions emphasize visual recall, orientation, and task-based cognitive stimulation, yet emotionally salient relational voice remains underused as a structured intervention mechanism. A growing body of evidence indicates that affectively encoded emotional responses can persist even after declarative memory for the events that produced them has faded. Building on this evidence, the paper advances a conceptual contribution: familiar relational voice — the voice of an attachment figure — is proposed to function as a cognitive anchor that may support emotional continuity, identity preservation, relational connection, and orientation even as episodic memory weakens. The paper introduces the VOCES Framework (Voz Orientada a la Continuidad, Emoción y Sostén), a culturally integrative, dignity-centered model that positions relational voice, emotional encoding, narrative continuity, and ritualized support as stabilizing mechanisms for identity continuity. The framework synthesizes research across auditory neuroscience, emotional memory, narrative identity, person-centered care, attachment theory, and healthcare communication; it does not claim that voice alters disease processes. MemoriGems is presented as one applied illustration of the framework. The paper concludes by outlining the research directions — including mixed-methods, feasibility, and implementation studies — needed to empirically evaluate voice-centered approaches to identity preservation in early cognitive decline.

articles.title: Influence campaigns in a custom social media platform affect beliefs, trust, and engagement
articles.authors: Manikya Alister; Keith Ransom; Andrew Perfors
articles.abstract: Despite growing concerns about how social media use can affect people's beliefs and behavior, estimating its causal impact is difficult. Here we present a novel method for studying social media effects using our own bespoke social media platform built using an isolated Mastodon server. Our platform allowed participants to interact much as they would on typical social media. Critically however, we controlled who could use the platform, which features it exposed, and we measured people's beliefs and attitudes before and after using the platform. This allowed us to more closely approximate the ecological validity of naturally occurring social-media data, while retaining the ability to measure variables and infer causation. Participants interacted over several days in three between-subject conditions (total N=311): a Control condition in which people engaged on the platform with no external influence, and two "troll" conditions (Left and Right) in which a small number of pre-planned posts sharing typical talking points from one political side were covertly made by us. We found that  our minimal influence campaigns resulted in statistically credible effects on engagement, beliefs, perceptions of others, and experience on the platform. More broadly, this work reveals the utility of our novel approach for studying social media effects.

articles.title: Am I Anxious or Rejected?  Measuring Implicit Associations in Social Anxiety
articles.authors: Mackenna Pattison; Dalainey H. Drakes; Eldar Eftekhari; Saray Velert-Jiménez; Nancy Bahl; Cynthia-Maria Kanaan; Allison Ouimet
articles.abstract: Social anxiety research has primarily relied on explicit self-report measures, which are vulnerable to response biases. Implicit measures have been used to examine underlying mechanisms of social anxiety (e.g., automatic associations). However, debate remains about their validity and utility. Prior research suggests that individuals with social anxiety are slower to associate the self with social acceptance-related words. We investigated whether the Implicit Association Test (IAT), using rejection vs. acceptance and anxiety vs. calm words, predicts anxiety during a speech task beyond explicit measures. We also tested whether concurrent facial electromyography (EMG) activity adds validity evidence for the IAT.
