Further, across the various direct learning outcomes, studies often did not include enough information to determine the comparability of conditions. For the most common learning outcome (i.e., ChatGPT > Control), comparisons often involved a confound between conditions as well as missing information about instructional features. Therefore, the benefits of ChatGPT must be interpreted with caution at the present time, and more research is needed to determine how, for whom, and under what pedagogical conditions ChatGPT can improve learning.

articles.title: Towards a Colonial Civil Sphere: A Critical Systematic Review of Civil Sphere Theory in Colonial and Postcolonial Contexts
articles.authors: Indra Bhaskar Mishra; Devesh Pandey
articles.abstract: Jeffrey C. Alexander’s Civil Sphere Theory (CST) has become one of the most influential frameworks in contemporary cultural sociology for understanding how solidarity, inclusion, and democratic life are culturally constituted. Yet CST’s applicability beyond the Western liberal democratic contexts, from which it emerged, remains underexamined. This position paper undertakes a critical theoretical analysis of the scholarly literature engaging with Alexander’s The Civil Sphere (2006) and its subsequent extensions by drawing on a systematic review of 41 studies identified through Web of Science and Scopus. This analysis identifies four structural limitations of CST that render it inadequate for analyzing colonial and postcolonial contexts, namely, Euro-American centric universalism, a liberal democratic precondition, nation-state boundedness, and the erasure of colonial power relations. Based on these findings, the article proposes a Colonial Civil Sphere (CCS) framework, built upon the conceptual pillars of constitutive contradiction, structured partial inclusion, constrained civil agency, and coloniality as persisting structure. The CCS framework reorients analysis from CST’s civil repair to civil construction, offering a theoretically grounded approach for understanding how civil life is constituted with, under, and against colonial domination. This article concludes by outlining implications for future research on colonial and postcolonial civil societies in the Global South.

articles.title: Overcoming construction constraints for the supply of new detached and high-rise housing
articles.authors: Megan Robinson; Andrea Sharam; Ali Zolghadr; Louise Dorignon; Ron Wakefield; Ehsan Gharaie; Mehrdad Arashpour; Peter Fairbrother; Anil Sawhney; Mohammad Mojtahedi
articles.abstract:
This Inquiry provides the first significant examination of the Australian construction sector’s ability to deliver both detached and high-rise housing. It analyses construction workflows, markets, regulation, workforce, technologies and supply chains.

The housing construction industry in Australia is at crisis point. The rate of Australia’s detached housing output has been largely static since at least 1980. Apartment construction can lift in response to demand, but output is volatile. There is no overarching strategy aimed at addressing housing construction constraints. This Inquiry provides eight interconnected options for policymakers and industry.

articles.title: Dissipative Representations: A Trajectorial Approach to Language and Identity Research
articles.authors: Luis Escobar L.-Dellamary
articles.abstract:
This paper develops Dissipative Representations (DiRe) as a trajectorial approach to lan-
guage research, identity studies, and cognitive sciences that dissolves dualistic thinking at its
root. Grounded in a consciousness-first monism—the recognition that experience, not matter, is
fundamental—DiRe treats the medium of meaning-making as a topology of weighted dispositions
rather than a substance to be named. Representations, under this approach, are characterized
by dispositional flexibility, provisional utility, relational dynamics, and critical resistance to ob-
jectification. The approach synthesizes Analytic Idealism, Decolonial Theory, and trajectorial
analysis within the Trace & Trajectory Framework (TTF) to provide researchers with tools that
honor the dynamic and emergent nature of meaning-making without sacrificing analytical rigor.
Trajectorial Dissipative Representations (Tra_DiRe) bridge foundational ontology and applied
analysis, while the orthogonal distinction between structural configuration (λ) and epistemic
access (σ) refines representational granularity. Dissipation itself is recast as the observable ef-
fect of a trajectorial mechanics: the rate at which representational coherence degrades when
the sustaining discursive ecology shifts or folds. The significance of this work extends toward a
transformative epistemological shift with applications for decolonizing knowledge systems and
revitalizing genuine diversity in approaches to intersubjective meaning-making.

articles.title: Poverty, educational attainment, and loss aversion: An analysis with prospect theory focusing on the loss aversion and forming reference point
articles.authors: Kazuhiro Kezuka; Ryo Suzuki
articles.abstract: The impact of financial assets on the decision to enter university has been studied in terms of the ability to pay tuition fees and invest in post-school education; however, the impact of assets on the decision-making process has not been fully investigated. We constructed a model based on prospect theory, focusing on the heterogeneity of loss aversion by assets and forming a reference point, and examined the relationship between assets and the decision to enter university (more specifically, taking an entrance exam). The results are twofold: 1) students from low-income households are more likely to identify themselves as those who should not enter universities and are likely not to choose to enter universities; 2) a decrease in the cost of preparing for entrance exams relaxes the threshold for taking the entrance exam, while a decrease in tuition does not always relax the threshold.

articles.title: Gendered Expectations of Representation: Do Constituents Prefer Women to be Locally-Oriented?
articles.authors: Tabitha Koch
articles.abstract: Gender and politics scholars have found women legislators to be more district-oriented than their male colleagues, often arguing that this behavior reflects strategic efforts to secure reelection. Yet no research has directly examined whether citizens expect women representatives to prioritize district-related activities or reward them for doing so. I argue that gender stereotypes portraying women as more communal lead voters to expect greater attention to local representation from women and to penalize them more harshly when they neglect district responsibilities. To test these expectations, I field a survey experiment in which respondents allocate a hypothetical U.S. House member’s time across national policymaking, securing local funding, and constituent service. Respondents then evaluate the same representative after reading a news-story vignette describing them as either attentive or inattentive to district needs. Contrary to expectations, voters do not hold gendered expectations about representational priorities nor do they penalize women more for inattentiveness.

articles.title: Climate Adaptation in the Lens of Frame Assemblages
articles.authors: Vanja Falck; Ivan Puga-Gonzalez; LeRon Shults
articles.abstract: People use frames, in Erving Goffman's sense, to make sense of encounters. Across Europe, the International Council for Local Environmental Initiatives (ICLEI) connects researchers, facilitators, implementers, and politicians on climate adaptation, yet knowledge reaches municipal practice only when participants adequately recognise each other's frames---which they often do not. Analysing 20 interviews, we show how frames embedded in assemblages (frame-assemblages) both obstruct and open up adaptation, with bottlenecks arising not only from scarce resources but from how situations are framed. We then outline a second use: derived from interview data, frame-assemblages act as empirically grounded, state-dependent filters on agents' capacities, offering a path from qualitative analysis to multi-agent social simulation.

articles.title: Exhaustion, Not Burnout: The Case for an Upstream Mechanism as Stress Science's Core Construct
articles.authors: Jonathan Hoover
articles.abstract: Burnout is among the most studied phenomena in occupational health, yet after five decades it lacks a consensual definition, a validated diagnostic threshold, and a demonstrated boundary from depression. This article approaches that difficulty not from burnout's weakness but from the strength of its core—exhaustion. Exhaustion is one of the best-established constructs in the psychological and stress sciences: it is measurable and performance-degrading in the cognitive-fatigue literature, it limits endurance in the psychobiology of performance, it prospectively predicts hard clinical endpoints such as myocardial infarction, and it is the most reliable and predictive dimension of every major burnout model. The instructive collapse of ego depletion—a depletion construct that failed rigorous replication—throws exhaustion's robustness into relief. I then pose a question the field has not squarely faced: is it adaptive to keep its most robust construct subordinate to a superordinate syndrome it cannot defend? I argue that it is not, and that the subordination is sustained by a taxonomic bid for scientific legitimacy and by a connotative accident of naming. I advance a constructive alternative that inverts the usual causal picture: rather than the terminal end of a stress chain, exhaustion is better understood as an upstream, trans-diagnostic, generative mechanism whose sustained depletion predisposes to depression, cardiovascular disease, and persistent cognitive impairment. Treating exhaustion, rather than burnout, as the field's core construct relocates explanatory weight onto defensible ground and dissolves several long-standing disputes.

articles.title: Economic horizontal inequality is linked to conflict persistence, not onset: High-resolution evidence from satellite-derived wealth measures in Africa
articles.authors: Connor T. Jerzak; Adel Daoud; Johannes Fagerlind
articles.abstract: Conflict research links horizontal inequality—systematic inequalities between identity groups—to armed violence, but it remains unclear whether economic inequality predicts conflict outbreak or instead shapes conflict dynamics after violence becomes plausible. We revisit this question in Africa using high-resolution satellite-derived International Wealth Index estimates to measure economic horizontal inequality among politically relevant ethnic groups and local wealth shocks. In group-year models, economic horizontal inequality is not statistically associated with conflict onset, while political marginalization is a stronger predictor. By contrast, economic horizontal inequality is associated with active-rebel group-years and higher casualty intensity among active-conflict group-years. A spatiotemporal counterfactual analysis finds that dense local wealth-shock scenarios are not associated with more conflict events on average, but estimated conditional contrasts become positive in areas with large absolute economic horizontal inequality. Economic horizontal inequality may therefore matter less as a general trigger than as a condition shaping conflict persistence, severity, and shock vulnerability.

articles.title: Umgang mit Emotionen von diskriminierten Personen in der Verbraucher:innen-Beratung: Eine qualitative Untersuchung von Beratungsstrategien
articles.authors: ConPolicy Institut für Verbraucherpolitik; Marlene Münsch; Sophia T. Dasch; Julius Rauber; Jule Niemeyer; Tammo Schmidt
articles.abstract:
Die vorliegende qualitative Studie untersucht, wie Beratungsorganisationen emotionale Belastungen diskriminierter Verbraucher:innen wahrnehmen und in der Beratung bearbeiten. Ziel ist es, Einblicke in bestehende Beratungspraktiken, organisationale Herausforderungen und Entwicklungsbedarfe zu geben.
Die Untersuchung basiert auf zwei methodischen Zugängen: einer Akteursfeldanalyse von 91 Beratungsorganisationen sowie 15 leitfadengestützten Expert:inneninterviews mit Beratenden aus verschiedenen Marktsektoren, darunter allgemeine Verbraucherberatung, Wohnungsmarkt, Finanzdienstleistungen, Gesundheitswesen, digitale Märkte sowie Kultur- und Freizeitmärkte. Die Interviews wurden inhaltlich-strukturierend ausgewertet.
Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass Diskriminierung in allen untersuchten Marktsektoren vorkommt und Verbraucher:innen entlang sozialer Kategorien wie Alter, Behinderung, Geschlecht, sexueller Orientierung, Herkunft oder Religion betrifft. In Beratungsgesprächen wird Diskriminierung jedoch selten ausdrücklich benannt, sondern zeigt sich häufig implizit in den geschilderten Anliegen. Wie offen sie thematisiert wird, hängt unter anderem vom Spezialisierungsgrad der Organisation ab.
Emotionen sind ein zentraler Bestandteil der Beratungssituation. Beratende berichten besonders häufig von Wut, Angst, Verzweiflung, Scham und Traurigkeit. Positive Emotionen wie Hoffnung oder das Gefühl, verstanden zu werden, entstehen oft erst im Verlauf der Beratung. Emotionen beeinflussen damit sowohl das Erleben der Ratsuchenden als auch Verlauf und Dauer der Gespräche.
Im Umgang mit emotionalen Belastungen nutzen Beratende unterschiedliche Strategien, darunter Empathie, Validierung, aktives Zuhören, Deeskalation, Wissensvermittlung sowie sach- und lösungsorientierte Unterstützung. Emotionale Anerkennung und Sachorientierung schließen sich dabei nicht aus; vielmehr kann das Aufgreifen von Emotionen eine Voraussetzung für erfolgreiche Problembearbeitung sein. Besonders bei Diskriminierungserfahrungen spielt Empowerment eine wichtige Rolle, um Handlungsmöglichkeiten aufzuzeigen und Ratsuchende zu stärken.
Gleichzeitig wird der Umgang mit Emotionen und Diskriminierung meist erfahrungsbasiert, informell und über kollegialen Austausch erlernt. Verbindliche Leitlinien, fachliche Standards und Fortbildungen fehlen häufig. Hinzu kommen strukturelle Herausforderungen wie Zeit- und Personalmangel, Sprachbarrieren und komplexe Problemlagen.
Insgesamt verdeutlichen die Befunde, dass Diskriminierung und Emotionen in der Verbraucher:innenberatung eine wichtige, aber oft implizite Rolle spielen. Die Ergebnisse sprechen für eine stärkere Verankerung diskriminierungs- und emotionssensibler Kompetenzen in Ausbildung, Fortbildung und Organisationsentwicklung sowie für eine engere Zusammenarbeit mit spezialisierten Beratungsangeboten.

articles.title: Marrying In vs. Marrying Out: Comparing Trajectories  of Functional Health of Exogamous and Endogamous Immigrant Unions in the U.S.
articles.authors: Aitor Garcia-Aguirre; Lucia Fernandez-Melero; Silvia Loi
articles.abstract:
While the Healthy Immigrant Paradox documents an initial health advantage among the foreign-born, ample evidence shows that they present an accelerated decline in comparison to the native-born. However, heterogeneities in these patterns of aging by different migrant groups remain largely understudied. This study addresses this gap by examining how marital assimilation stratifies functional health trajectories among U.S. immigrants. Using longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and growth curve models, we compare the accumulation of Activities of Daily Living (ADL) limitations between immigrants in intramarried (same-origin) and intermarried (native-partner) unions.

Our results reveal distinct stratification by union type. We find that intermarried immigrants present "premium," allowing immigrants to maintain health trajectories indistinguishable from the native-born population. In contrast, intramarried married immigrants experience accelerated functional decline, a disadvantage that is particularly pronounced among women. Furthermore, we find support for a "Substitution Hypothesis," where marriage to a native-born partner effectively substitutes for the integration benefits typically accrued through duration of residence. These findings showcase that the "immigrant health advantage" and its ensuing erosion is not uniform but is conditional on the type of union, duration of residence and gender.

articles.title: Warum Beschäftigte KI am Arbeitsplatz seltener nutzen: Gründe für den Rückgang der beruflichen KI-Nutzung in Deutschland
articles.authors: Marco Lünich
articles.abstract: Der Kurzbericht untersucht das Ausmaß und die Veränderung der beruflichen Nutzung künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) unter Erwerbstätigen in Deutschland. Grundlage ist eine quotierte Online-Befragung (CAWI) von rund 2.585 Erwerbstätigen. Im Mittelpunkt steht, wie sich die berufliche KI-Nutzung in den letzten drei Monaten verändert hat, welche Gründe für eine verringerte Nutzung genannt werden und wie eine Zu- oder Abnahme mit individuellen und organisationsbezogenen Merkmalen zusammenhängt. Die Mehrheit berichtet von einer gleichbleibenden Nutzung. Insgesamt überwiegen Zunahmen, während eine Verringerung nur einen kleinen Teil der Erwerbstätigen betrifft. Eine rückläufige Nutzung ist mit kritischeren KI-Einstellungen, geringerer subjektiver Kompetenz und organisationaler Unterstützung sowie mit fehlendem Mehrwert, unzuverlässigen Ergebnissen und Datenschutzbedenken verbunden. Zugleich zeigen sich soziale Unterschiede: Höherqualifizierte erhöhen ihre Nutzung eher, geringer Qualifizierte verringern sie vergleichsweise häufiger. Damit stellt sich die Frage, ob KI bestehende Ungleichheiten am Arbeitsplatz abbaut oder verstärkt.

articles.title: Social and health risk factors for miscarriage: a population-based study using French healthcare records
articles.authors: Marie-Caroline Compans; Hélène Malmanche; Heini Väisänen
articles.abstract:
Objective: To study social and clinical factors associated with (early or late) miscarriage, while accounting for births and induced abortions.
Design: Population-based analysis of French healthcare records from 2015 to 2023.
Subjects : Pregnancies among women aged 15-49 that resulted in birth, miscarriage or induced abortion.
Main Outcome Measures: Predicted probabilities for a pregnancy to result in birth, induced abortion, or miscarriage, including early (<14 gestational weeks) or late (14-22 gestational weeks) miscarriage. The probabilities are estimated using multinomial regression models controlling for key socio-demographic and health factors. 
Results: Eight percent of the studied pregnancies were miscarriages and among them, seven percent occurred at a late gestational age. Adjusted results for socio-demographic factors show age below 19 or above 40 were associated with higher predicted probabilities for miscarriage: while the predicted probabilities were below 10% for the age groups in the middle, they were 14.0% [13.9%;14.2%] for adolescents and 16.0% [15.9%;16.1%] for those in their early 40s. There were no differences in overall miscarriage risk between rural, peri-urban and urban residential areas, or by financial precarity status, except for late miscarriages where risk was higher among those in a precarious financial situation. Regarding past reproductive history, miscarriage was more likely after the use of medically assisted reproduction, with the predicted probabilities for this group being 14.9% [14.7%;15.0%] compared to 7.5% [7.4%;7.5%] for those without. Previous births or induced abortions were associated with lower predicted probabilities of miscarriage, whereas previous miscarriages were associated with an increased probability of miscarriage (e.g. 12.5% [12.3%;12.8%] after multiple miscarriages and 7.3% [7.3%;7.3%] if no previous miscarriage). Chronic diseases were each associated with slightly higher predicted probabilities of miscarriage, with exceptionally high association for kidney failure (17.0% [15.1%;19.1%]).
Conclusion: No social inequalities were observed for early miscarriage risk, but the risk of late miscarriage was more important for financially precarious than other women. Regarding health factors, chronic kidney disease was particularly strongly associated with elevated miscarriage risk, while all included chronic diseases increased the risk somewhat.

articles.title: Teachers’ Mental Models in Secondary Education and Their Implications for Teacher Professional Development: A Systematic Literature Review
articles.authors: Annemarieke Gerarda Helena Maria Schepers; Peter Verkoeijen; Dominique M.A. Sluijsmans
articles.abstract: Teachers often struggle to reinterpret familiar situations and enact new insights in practice. Mental models are central in this process, as they shape how teachers interpret and regulate classroom situations. However, the literature lacks conceptual clarity regarding mental models, and coherence regarding their explicitation, change and support through teacher professional development (TPD). This systematic literature review synthesizes findings from 22 studies to address this fragmentation. The results show that mental models are cognitive representations shaped by knowledge structures, beliefs, and assumptions. Although methods exist to make mental models explicit and to support change processes in TPD, understanding of how these elements interrelate is still underdeveloped. Consequently, guidelines for aligning methods, processes, and goals in TPD addressing mental models remain limited. We, therefore, provide a foundation for a more integrated, design-oriented understanding of how TPD can support changes in teachers’ mental models. Further research is needed to ensure alignment in practice.

articles.title: Road Violence and Perceptions of Safety among Pedestrians and Cyclists
articles.authors: Jose Pina-Sánchez; Alexander Trinidad; Ian Loader
articles.abstract: This registered report investigates whether involvement in road traffic collisions meaningfully shapes pedestrians’ and cyclists’ perceptions of safety. Drawing on criminological insights - particularly the fear‑victimisation paradox - the study explores the common policy assumption that reducing collisions alone improves subjective safety. Using ESRA2 survey data from 24 European countries, the analysis estimates both average and conditional treatment effects of collision experience on perceived safety, accounting for vulnerability (age, gender) and exposure (active travel frequency). The study employs equivalence testing and counterfactual modelling to assess whether victims’ perceptions differ from non‑victims’. Findings will clarify whether collision reduction strategies are sufficient to encourage active travel or whether broader interventions addressing vulnerability and environmental cues are required.

articles.title: Die Rettungsmaschine. Sexarbeit, Anti-Trafficking und extraterritoriale Strafmacht in Südostasien. Eine theoretische Synthese.
articles.authors: Susanne Bleier Wilp
articles.abstract:
This paper develops a theoretical synthesis of sex work and anti-trafficking
power in Southeast Asia and argues that the region reveals US extraterritorial
power in its fourth and most contradictory mode. Where a companion paper
on the Global North found that power exercised through platform law
(FOSTA-SESTA), a paper on the Global South through the PEPFAR antiprostitution pledge, and a paper on Eastern Europe through the abrupt
withdrawal of funding, Southeast Asia shows it as evaluative power: the US
State Department's annual Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report ranks
governments by tier and can trigger sanctions, rewarding the criminalisation,
raids and rescue operations that Bernstein (2018) has theorised as carceral
feminism and militarised humanitarianism. The paradox is that the same US
power that financed harm reduction through PEPFAR simultaneously
incentivises criminalisation through the TIP Report - while the strongest
available evidence, a quasi-experimental study from East Java (Cameron,
Seager and Shah 2021), shows that criminalisation increases sexually
transmitted infections among sex workers by 58 percent. Drawing on this
evidence, on Weitzer's (2023) ethnography of the Thai sex industry, and on
Parmanand's (2019) study of the Philippine Sex Workers Collective, the paper
makes three claims. First, the anti-trafficking architecture functions as a
machine that produces the victims it claims to rescue, extending Agustin's
(2007) concept of the rescue industry into its operating logic. Second, this
machine structurally suffocates the self-organisation that could carry reform,
because criminalisation prevents legal registration and funding. Third,
Thailand's ongoing effort to repeal its 1996 Prostitution Act is the Southeast
Asian counterpart to the Belgian and South African experiments, in which the
sex worker organisation Empower explicitly demands decriminalisation
rather than regulated legalisation. The evidence base is uneven: Thailand and
the Philippines carry the analysis, while Vietnam appears only as an evidencebased contextual case.

articles.title: The Rescue Machine Sex Work, Anti-Trafficking, and Extraterritorial Carceral Power in Southeast Asia. A Theoretical Synthesis.

articles.title: The IP Paradox for New Zealand Scientific Start-Ups: Navigating Value and Impediment in Technology Transfer
articles.authors: Sam Mutsamwira
articles.abstract:
This study examines how scientist-entrepreneurs in New Zealand experience and navigate intellectual property (IP) during the technology transfer process. Using interpretative phenomenological analysis, the study draws on semi-structured interviews with fourteen scientist-entrepreneurs, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis. The findings reveal a central IP Paradox; IP is simultaneously an indispensable prerequisite for technology transfer and a significant impediment. Useful theories, the Innovation Incentive Theory, Knowledge Spillover Theory of Entrepreneurship, and Resource-Based View, only partially explain this phenomenon, as managing IP introduces profound strategic tensions, costs, and uncertainties. The analysis elucidates the IP Paradox for scientific start-ups, which complements and adds on to these dominant theoretical frameworks, and then develops an IP Navigation Matrix as a sense-making and decision-support tool grounded in entrepreneurs’ lived experience. This provides a nuanced understanding of IP’s dual role, offering direct managerial and policy implications for improving technology transfer, supporting academic entrepreneurship, and fostering innovation in New Zealand and other small open economies. The findings also provide practical insights for IP practitioners advising scientific ventures in New Zealand.

Keywords: intellectual property protection; scientific start-ups; patents; trade secrets; technology transfer; New Zealand

articles.title: Every Methodology is a Weapon if you Hold it Right: Union-Led Well-Being Measurement as an Act of Collective Resistance
articles.authors: Jon Mendel; Taylor G. Hill
articles.abstract: Workplace well-being surveys are typically led by employers in a hierarchical, top-down way, treating distress as a problem on the individual scale rather than a collective condition. Drawing on Marston et al.’s (2005) critique of hierarchical scale, this paper reimagines well-being measurement by developing a democratic practice of industrial participation and epistemic resistance that offers more horizontal points of entry. As part of a union-led case study at the University of Dundee, Scotland, we examine how a community-driven initiative co-designed and administered a well-being survey during a period of acute institutional crisis (N = 84). Survey findings indicated near-universal burnout with widespread physical and psychological ill-health, reports of excessive unsustainable workloads, low autonomy, and eroded organisational trust. The paper shows that that participatory data practices can represent horizontal infrastructures of care and that these practices work as both evidence of harm and as revolutionary theory in Harvey’s (2009: 152) terms: engaging with status quo ideas like well-being to provide “them with real content, and using them to identify real choices immanent in the present”. We draw on theories of pragmatism to discuss how radicalising well-being measurement extends industrial democracy by shifting the means of knowledge production: workers define and evidence their own realities, transforming surveys from tools of managerial oversight into practices of solidarity and weapons for resistance. To resist the use of well-being measurement as a tool of hierarchical government, we aim to show that every methodology can be a weapon if you use it right.

articles.title: Parental separation in childhood and development of political party identification in young adulthood
articles.authors: Lena Wagner
articles.abstract: Party identification is widely recognised as a pillar of democratic stability and a driver of political participation rooted in family socialisation. Although parental separation has become increasingly common across Europe, little is known about its implications for political socialisation. This study examines how parental separation during childhood (ages 0-15) affects the probability of identifying with any political party across the developmental trajectory of young adulthood (ages 18-25) by estimating logistic mixed-effects growth models on longitudinal mother-child dyadic data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (years 2001-2024; N = 2,770). Growing up with a partisan mother emerges as the strongest predictor of party identification, while maternal education exerts an independent effect and parental separation shows a modest negative association. Effects are largely confined to initial levels at age 18, pointing to early and persistent stratification. Going beyond average effects, results indicate that separation weakens mother-child transmission, particularly following early-childhood separation, while having little impact among offspring of apartisan mothers. Additional analyses suggest that weakened transmission cannot be explained by father absence alone but may reflect complex post-separation family dynamics.

articles.title: What makes or breaks newly-cohabs? Couples’ gender attitudinal pairings and their union trajectories
articles.authors: Daniele Florean; Natalie Nitsche
articles.abstract: While declining marriage and rising cohabitation are not new, less partnering, more breakups, and rising singlehood are novel and poorly understood trends. How newly cohabiting couples' joint gender attitudes predict their relationship trajectories, and whether this varies across social contexts, is hence an important yet underresearched question. Using data from the German Family Panel (pairfam), we follow 1,297 newly formed couples, investigating how their gender attitudinal pairings evolve and predict breakups or marriage transitions, leveraging East-West German gender climate differences to assess contextual moderation. Our findings extend the literature in three ways. First, gender climate context matters for marriage transitions: among West but not East German couples, joint traditionalism is associated with more than twice the marriage transition rate of attitudinally mismatched couples. Second, attitudinal convergence among initially mismatched couples (the majority in our sample) emerges as the strongest predictor of both higher marriage rates and lower breakup risks across both regions. Third, the gender normative context appears to interact with attitudinal pairings in whether couples marry but not in whether they stay together. This suggests intra-couple psychological processes are a key predictor of family formation dynamics and deserve more attention in demographic research.

articles.title: The Measurement Crisis in Cognitive Warfare Defence: Evaluating Single-Layer Countermeasures across Democratic Societies
articles.authors: Cezar Vasilescu
articles.abstract:
State-sponsored cognitive warfare has emerged as a defining cross-national security challenge, systematically targeting the information environments of democratic societies and allied institutions. Yet despite the proliferation of defensive countermeasures since 2020, systematic evidence evaluation remains critically limited. This research examines four major individual intervention categories (prebunking and inoculation theory, artificial intelligence detection technologies, media literacy programmes, and rapid response systems) through structured evidence synthesis applying adapted GRADE criteria.
Two research objectives guide the analysis: evaluating empirical evidence quality and identifying measurement limitations that systematically overestimate operational effectiveness; and analysing performance gaps between laboratory conditions and real-world deployment. Evidence reveals substantial variation in empirical support across countermeasure categories. Prebunking demonstrates the strongest evidence base, with large-scale field studies showing 55-60% improvements in manipulation detection. AI detection systems show 45-50% accuracy degradation from laboratory to operational conditions due to adversarial adaptation.
The research identifies a fundamental measurement problem: over 89% of studies analysed measure capabilities rather than behaviours, creating systematic overestimation of intervention effectiveness. These findings provide evidence-grounded guidance for national security planners, defence ministries, and NATO member states allocating resources to cognitive defence, emphasising behavioural validation as a prerequisite for operational confidence.

articles.title: Communal Activities as Intercultural Communication Strategies of Social Actors in Developing Social Cohesion in Sudiroprajan
articles.authors: Buddy Riyanto; Andrik Purwasito; Andre Noevi Rahmanto; Sri Hastjarjo
articles.abstract: This article examines communal activities as intercultural communication strategies used by local social actors to develop social cohesion in Sudiroprajan, Surakarta, Indonesia. Sudiroprajan is a multicultural urban neighborhood in which Javanese residents, Chinese Indonesians, Javanese-Chinese descendants, and communities with diverse religious, generational, occupational, and socio-economic backgrounds interact in everyday life. Using a qualitative approach within a constructivist paradigm and a grounded theory strategy, this study draws on observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation of community practices. The findings show that Grebeg Sudiro, Barongsai Macan Putih, neighborhood collective work, Kampung Pelangi, the Harapan Kita Waste Bank, the Suka Maju Women Farmers Group, and the Sinar Mentari Climate Village Program operate as communicative arenas where residents encounter difference, negotiate meanings, coordinate roles, reproduce local values, and create shared experiences. Social actors, including community leaders, neighborhood administrators, religious figures, women’s groups, youth, cultural activists, and environmental organizers, act as initiators, mobilizers, facilitators, mediators, and interpreters of meaning. The article argues that communal activities are not merely socio-cultural or environmental programs; they constitute an infrastructure of intercultural communication that transforms diversity into social capital, strengthens trust, and supports inclusive community identity.

articles.title: Enabling Sustainability Transitions in the Semiconductor Domain: Designing a Transition Practice–Education Cycle
articles.authors: Hiromi Kimoto; Maoko Fujisaki; Keito Inoue; Norio Kamitsubo; Sota Takagi; Kohei Saito; Takumi Ohashi
articles.abstract: Semiconductors are enabling technologies whose innovation is largely governed by technical roadmaps, leaving limited infrastructure for the normative deliberation and capability-building required for sustainability transitions. This paper asks how transition agenda formation can be connected to university-based education and project formation in the semiconductor sector. Drawing on Transition Design and Transition Management, we conceptualize the Transition Practice–Education Cycle (TPEC), a process framework that iteratively links transition agenda formation with industry and domain frontrunners, university-based Transition Design education, and project formation with committed stakeholders. Using Research through Design, we report an initial TPEC implementation at Institute of Science Tokyo in the semiconductor domain. The analysis identifies two translation functions absent from the initial design: Agenda-to-Education Translation and Project Translation and Validation. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a revised TPEC framework that embeds both as explicit design functions. The study also suggests Transition-oriented Semiconductor Capability as a potential educational goal for enabling technology sectors.

articles.title: Beyond the Takeover: Youth Gatherings, Urban Public Space, and the Racialization of Disorder in Chicago
articles.authors: Almethia C. Franklin
articles.abstract:
In recent years, Chicago has witnessed a significant rise in large-scale youth gatherings in high-visibility public spaces. Labeled "teen takeovers" in dominant media and policy discourse, these events are almost exclusively framed as public safety threats requiring law enforcement response. This paper argues that this framing is both analytically insufficient and politically consequential. Drawing on preliminary media and news analysis, an emerging qualitative research agenda, and a multi-disciplinary theoretical framework, this paper reframes youth gatherings as social phenomena that reveal fundamental dynamics of race, space, territorial boundary, and urban belonging. We identify three dimensions that existing scholarship has not yet systematically examined: (1) the role of social media and digital technology in organizing, escalating, and documenting these events; (2) the apparent dissolution of hyperlocal territorial boundaries historically maintained by street organizations in Chicago; and (3) the variation in form, activity, and framing of analogous youth gatherings across U.S. cities. We situate these dimensions within a five-part theoretical architecture drawing on moral panic theory, critical criminology, spatial theory, Black cultural studies, and the sociology of punishment. We conclude by presenting a research agenda for empirical investigation and discussing the implications of this work for policy and community response.

Keywords: youth gatherings, teen takeovers, urban public space, moral panic, territorial boundaries, Chicago, racialization, social media, cultural criminology

articles.title: Algorithmic Decision Making in Medical Diagnosis: Understanding The Ambiguity Present Within Australian Law and 'Explainable Artificial Intelligence'
articles.authors: James Scheibner; Khevalin Parekh
articles.abstract: This paper assesses whether Australian medical device regulation, tort and privacy law impose a requirement for artificial intelligence based Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) to be explainable. The paper analyses the concept of ‘explainability’ through a framework developed by Ferretti, Schneider and Blasimme (2018) which divides algorithmic opacity into three categories: lack of disclosure, epistemic opacity and explanatory opacity. These three categories of opacity concern varying levels of understanding of algorithmic outcomes by different audiences. This paper first examines whether medical device regulations in Australia impose a duty on medical device manufacturers to ensure machine learning powered CDSS tools are explainable. This paper then assesses whether Australian negligence law imposes an equivalent obligation on medical practitioners. Finally, this paper examines whether recent Australian privacy law reforms impose a requirement of explainability. This paper concludes that each of the three branches of law imposes a requirement for medical device manufacturers and practitioners to disclose when machine learning is used in CDSS tools. However, there is no further legal obligation to explain how these tools make decisions, or why they reach particular decisions.

articles.title: Internal Dispossession: A Sovereignty-Grounded Theory of the Harms of American Indian Identity Theft
articles.authors: Cynthia Greywolf
articles.abstract:
American Indian identity theft (self-indigenization, pretendianism) is usually treated as one
person’s deception. I argue that it is something larger. This article presents Internal
Dispossession Theory (IDT), a sovereignty-grounded theory of the harms of American Indian
identity theft. Its premise is that identity theft is the latest form of colonial dispossession: as
Native land and resources were taken, so too is the authority of tribal nations to say who belongs,
relocated from the nation onto individuals, institutions, and markets. That relocation produces
relational, structural, and epistemic harms that culminate in internal dispossession: the erosion of
a tribal nation’s capacity to define itself, lived also by the individual Native person whose place a
counterfeit takes. Stated as nine propositions and grounded in a sovereign autoethnography of a
documented case, IDT names a contemporary colonial mechanism. Its remedy is not institutional
gatekeeping but tribal self-determination.

articles.title: Islam, Reason and Modernity in Colonial India: a Comparative Study of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and Syed Ameer Ali
articles.authors: NAFIS HAIDER
articles.abstract:
The paper examines the debates around reason and rationality in Islam, particularly in the works of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and Syed Ameer Ali, locating their modernist articulation in the backdrop of socio-political context of colonial India. In the aftermath of the revolt of 1857, Muslims in India were subjected to institutional marginalisation, incarceration, civilisational stigma and intensified suspicion. As the orientalist discourse portrayed Muslims and Islam as an irrational, oriental and despotic tradition, it rendered Muslims political claims vulnerable to discrimination under colonial modernity. This crisis of political exclusion pushed for an articulation of Islam as a rational and ethical tradition. 
The paper argues that Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and Syed Ameer Ali reinterpreted Islam as a rational tradition which transcends mere theological category and served also as a political strategy of survival, locating Islam and Muslims as legitimate ethical civilisation. Sir Syed grounds his interpretation of Islam in a rationalist hermeneutics, through natural law and scientific reason which aimed at making Islamic tradition intelligible to colonial epistemology, enabling education, political participation and representation. Syed Ameer Ali while running on the similar thread, works along a parallel pathway of juridical and historical reasoning to defend Islam as a moral and constitutional epistemology. Though differing in methodology and approach, both thinkers rearticulated Islam as compatible with the changing world order. Through a comparative study of these two thinkers, the paper tries to identify the different and multiple rationalities within the framework of Islamic modernism in Colonial India.
The paper states that this political idiom of survival and legitimacy works in extending and reshaping Muslim reformist thought, reoriented debate on constitutional politics, representation and institutional arrangement in colonial India. By foregrounding reason as a political strategy, the paper contributes to the intellectual history of Islam in South Asia and the ways through which modernist Islamic discourse negotiated through power, exclusion and belongingness under colonial rule in India.

Keywords: Islam, Muslim, Colonialism, Modernity, Political exclusion, South Asia

articles.title: Does Carbon Pricing Outperform Command-and-Control Regulation? Firm-Level Evidence from Korea’s Dual Regulatory Framework
articles.authors: Pyung Kim
articles.abstract: This study exploits South Korea’s unique dual-policy, in which an emissions trading scheme (ETS) and a command-and-control program (Target Management System, TMS) operate in parallel, to compare carbon pricing with prescriptive regulation at the firm level. Using a difference-in-differences design on firm-level panel data from 2011 to 2022, I find that ETS-regulated firms reduced energy use by 5.8% to 8.8% and carbon emissions by 7.3% to 8.5% relative to TMS firms, while effects on carbon intensity were not robust. These reductions were strongest in the more market-oriented phases of the ETS, which featured allowance auctioning and benchmark-based allocation, pointing to the importance of incentive-based policy design.

articles.title: Projecting Intergenerational Family Structures  over the Life Course:  Empirical and Simulated Populations in Norway
articles.authors: Bettina Hünteler; Diego Alburez-Gutierrez
articles.abstract: Much existing research in the demography of kinship focuses on quantifying the number and characteristics of living kin, such as age and sex. We know less about which intergenerational family structures individuals experience throughout their life – for example, when and how long they are parents, children or experience overlap of multiple family generations – although this is important because such trajectories are heterogeneous, potentially producing inequalities in kinship availability across the life. We use simulated micro-level data to project generational placement trajectories for life courses of the complete population of Norway born 1960 and 2000. Our microsimulations use age-specific fertility and mortality rates from 1846 to 2100. First, we benchmark projected trajectories for the 1960 cohort against observed trajectories from empirical register data from 1960 to 2019. Second, we project full life-course trajectories, from age 0 to 100, for the 1960 and 2000 cohorts. Results from sequence analysis show that generational placement trajectories efficiently capture individual-level heterogeneity in intergen-erational kin availability and that results based on our simulated populations largely match those from empirical data. Over cohorts, typical generational placement trajectories will likely become more stable but “thinner”, with later (and shorter) demographic “(double) sandwiching” and increasingly frequent “fading family lines.” The analysis paves the path toward results on a global level and including projections for the future.

articles.title: The Weight of Precedent: Parties, Institutions, and Executive Norms
articles.authors: Daniel A. N. Goldstein; Collin Thomas Schumock
articles.abstract: Political executives often adhere to informal traditions established by their predecessors. Yet, without legal backing, elites have incentives to violate norms for political gain. Under what conditions do constraining executive norms persist and when are they abandoned? We address this question by using an infinite horizon formal model to analyze the maintenance of executive norms. We identify intra-party accountability and variation in patience among actors within the same party as significant for norm maintenance. We also detail how expectations about the expected behavior of out-of-power parties shape the willingness to violate norms while in office. The insights from the model enable us to classify a number of executive norms according to their fragility and to examine the trajectory of one norm in-depth: the two-term tradition of the American presidency. Our findings shed light on how informal institutions regulate executive behavior and advance our understanding of institutional stability and erosion.

articles.title: Indirect Influence: How Elite Attacks on Information Providers Affect Public Opinion Formation
articles.authors: Erik Peterson; Allison Michelle Nam Archer; Kishan Bhakta; SHO IZUMISAWA
articles.abstract: Attacks from politicians can dramatically reduce public trust in sources of expertise and information. We consider the consequences of such criticism and argue that by shaping which information providers their supporters consider credible, politicians can exert indirect influence over public opinion formation. In two survey experiments that link elite criticism of the media to other outcomes, we show politicians who discredit a media outlet cause their supporters to avoid the targeted news source and perceive more bias in its coverage. Partisan attacks also reduce the subsequent effect of the news source's coverage on public opinion, although people are unable to fully discount information from sources they deem untrustworthy due to this rhetoric. Looking beyond direct means of elite influence such as positional cues and policy arguments, we show how harming the reputations of information providers allows politicians to indirectly influence the views of their supporters.

articles.title: Mandatory AI Disclosure Sorts Products into Launch Failure: Evidence from Steam
articles.authors: Kenny Ching
articles.abstract: Platforms increasingly require firms to disclose when products incorporate generative artificial intelligence (AI). Existing evidence largely asks whether such disclosure changes consumer demand; we show that a complementary question—where demand is lost—is at least as important. Using a cross-section of 799 visual-novel games on Steam released early enough to observe a complete 90-day post-release window—of which 22% carry a platform-mandated AI-use disclosure—we show that the consumer response to AI disclosure is concentrated almost entirely on the extensive margin. Disclosed games are roughly twice as likely to obtain no early traction at all: the rate of zero day-30 reviews rises from 5.0% to 9.0%, an odds ratio of 2.14. Among games that do gain an audience, by contrast, the rate of subsequent review accumulation is statistically indistinguishable by disclosure status, and the continuous accumulation penalty is not robust to controls. Disclosed games that are reviewed receive ratings about six percentage points lower. The market response to disclosure is therefore not a uniform discount applied to every product, but a bimodal pattern: a higher probability of failing to launch, and modestly lower satisfaction among survivors. We discuss implications for the design of mandatory disclosure more broadly: when a label can determine whether a product is seen at all, the welfare consequences of disclosure differ sharply depending on whether it gently discounts demand or sorts products into launch failure, and on the producer incentives it sets in motion.

articles.title: SCIENTIFIC FACTS AS CIVILISATIONAL ACHIEVEMENTS: AN ASSESSMENT
articles.authors: Muhammad Abdul Khudus
articles.abstract: Are scientific facts civilisational achievements? Answering this requires clarifying both terms. Drawing on the classical Islamic tradition, namely, al-Fārābī’s virtuous city and the later frameworks of Ibn Khaldūn, Osman Bakar, Wan Mohd Nor Wan Daud, and al-Attas, we argue that a genuine civilisational achievement must engage the physical, mental, and spiritual dimensions of human flourishing, and, on al-Attas’s view, must stand in some relation to revealed Truth. We then characterise a “scientific fact” not as plain truth but as a proposition that is provisionally true: empirically constrained, communally validated, and open to revision. Using three “outdated facts” Pluto’s demotion, the abandonment of the luminiferous aether, and the discovery of additional states of matter, we show that scientific facts are revisable in structurally different ways: definitional, ontological, and enumerative. The deepest layer, the constituent framework or worldview, is never delivered by experiment; it is inherited from the civilisation that produces the science. Every scientific fact is therefore a civilisational achievement, requiring the madīnah, the ummah of inquirers, and a budaya ilmu. But when scientific claims overstep their evidential station and smuggle in an inherited metaphysics, the Muslim community is under no obligation to receive that metaphysics as fact. This, I suggest, is the real meaning of al-Attas’s de-westernization of knowledge: to accept what the instruments have honestly read from the book of creation, while declining the unexamined worldview wrapped around it.

articles.title: Psychological features of dispute content and public acceptance of AI in legal adjudication: evidence for systematic variation beyond individual differences
articles.authors: Masahiro Fujita; Eiichiro Watamura
articles.abstract: Public acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) in legal decision-making has been primarily explained through individual differences in personality traits and general attitudes toward technology. However, emerging evidence suggests that contextual features of legal disputes themselves may systematically influence preferences for AI versus human adjudicators. Across two studies with Japanese participants (N = 1,384 and N = 596), we examined whether psychological characteristics of dispute content—beyond demographics and individual traits—shape acceptability judgments for algorithmic adjudication. Study 1 employed exploratory factor analysis on acceptability ratings across 46 legal dispute vignettes, revealing a robust two-dimensional structure distinguishing interpersonal-relational disputes (where human adjudicators were strongly preferred) from institutional-procedural disputes (where AI acceptance was comparatively higher, though not surpassing human preference in most cases). Study 2 replicated this dimensional structure in an independent sample and demonstrated that experimentally manipulated contextual features—emotional involvement and prototypicality—systematically modulated acceptability judgments, with effects varying by dispositional trust, AI-specific attitudes, and gender. AI-specific expectations emerged as the strongest predictor of acceptance (η2 = 0.252), and a three-way interaction among emotional involvement, gender, and prototypicality indicated that contextual effects are moderated by individual characteristics. These findings suggest that the psychological features of dispute content constitute an overlooked dimension in AI acceptance research, extending beyond technology acceptance models to fundamental questions about how individuals construe social problems and allocate adjudicative authority. We discuss limitations related to measurement approaches, alternative psychological mechanisms, and directions for future research employing real-world case materials and direct assessment of cognitive processes.

articles.title: High resolution measures of preference-based local segregation for the United States, 2018-2023
articles.authors: Jiwon Jang; Dylan Shane Connor; Peter Rogerson; Daoqin Tong
articles.abstract: Neighborhood segregation is a strong driver of disparities in human well-being, yet traditional measures largely ignore the segregation experienced beyond residential neighborhoods. Recent human mobility-based measures have advanced this field by quantifying segregated mobility patterns when choosing travel destinations, but they are often confounded by spatial exposure (i.e., the demographic diversity of the neighborhoods locally reachable from one’s residence) rather than a behavioral preference for similarity. Without adjusting for this baseline exposure, such metrics largely act as proxies for the local residential environment, conflating limited demographic diversity in surrounding areas with active travel decisions to neighborhoods similar to one’s own. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Community Connectivity (CO-CONNECT) dataset, combining billions of anonymized cellphone location records with census tract-level socio-demographic attributes (2018-2023). The dataset operationalizes the Spatial Preference in Local Interaction (SPLIT) index, a local measure of segregation that quantifies the extent to which residents travel to socio-demographically similar neighborhoods, adjusted for the demographic similarity of surrounding neighborhoods. This framework explicitly separates travel decisions that exacerbate group-based segregation from segregation attributable to demographic composition alone, providing a high-resolution picture of mobility-based segregation and its temporal trends across the United States.

articles.title: The Suburb Disruption Cycle and Dorsett’s Law of Suburban Succession: A Theoretical Model of Residential Turnover and Suburban Reinvention
articles.authors: Mark Dorsett
articles.abstract:
This paper proposes the Suburb Disruption Cycle as a theoretical model for explaining
suburban transformation as a patterned process of disruption, reorganisation and
residential succession. Existing accounts of suburban change often emphasise particular
dimensions of transformation, including decline, gentrification, densification, migration,
financialisation, post-suburbanisation and symbolic revaluation. This paper synthesises
these dimensions into an eight-stage causal sequence: Current Residents, Disruption,
Housing Form, Affordability, Reputation, Business Ecology, Resident Turnover and New
Residents. From this sequence, the paper derives Dorsett’s Law of Suburban Succession:
sustained disruption within or upon a suburb produces residential succession when it
reorganises housing form, affordability, reputation and business ecology. The law is
advanced as a conditional sociological proposition rather than a deterministic claim. Its
purpose is to explain how new resident orders are produced through cumulative material,
economic, symbolic and commercial change. The paper develops the model conceptually
and applies it to St Kilda, Victoria, during its Riviera of Victoria life cycle from 1860 to
1910. The case demonstrates how transport access, gold-rush wealth, land speculation
and financial crisis contributed to housing transformation, rising exclusivity, reputational
elevation, leisure-oriented business development and the emergence of a new elite seaside
resident order. The paper contributes a middle-range theory of suburban reinvention that
can guide future historical, comparative and empirical research into suburban succession.

articles.title: Research on the Communication and Synergistic Development of Yao Medical Culture and Industry: A Case Study of Liannan Yao Medicine in Guangdong Province
articles.authors: shijie
articles.abstract: Against the backdrop of the "Healthy China" initiative and the rural revitalization strategy, the preservation and industrial development of Yao medical culture face both opportunities and deep-seated obstacles. Taking the Liannan Yao Autonomous County in Guangdong Province as a case study, this research systematically investigates the current state and challenges of the local Yao medicine industry through three methods: a questionnaire survey (238 valid responses), in-depth interviews (with 3 Yao medicine inheritors and 2 local cultural officials), and participant observation (15 days of fieldwork). The findings are threefold. First, while the local cultural identification rate with Yao medicine reaches as high as 78%, the actual utilization rate is only 55.5%, and the rate of choosing Yao medicine as the first option for medical treatment is as low as 3.6%, revealing a cognitive-practical paradox of "high identification, low consumption." Second, chi-square tests indicate a significant association between ethnic identity and usage behavior (χ² = 8.41, p < 0.01), as well as a significant divergence between trust and actual use (χ² = 28.94, p < 0.001). Third, the formation of this paradox can be attributed to a fourfold blockage: institutional access barriers, lack of product standardization, cognitive disconnection, and the strong substitution effect of modern medicine. The study proposes a five-dimensional synergistic development pathway—encompassing institutional supply, communication mechanisms, product transformation, cultural tourism integration, and industrial ecology—to transform Liannan's Yao medicine from a form of local knowledge into a competitive cultural and industrial asset.

articles.title: An Analytical Framework for the Assessment of Employment Impacts of Energy Transition
articles.authors: Rudeena Jabar; Anjali Sharma; Haritha Songola
articles.abstract: The potential employment generation is an important co-benefit and policy motivation to pursue energy transition. Empirical evidence suggests that energy transition leads to net employment gains. However, the job estimates vary across studies due to methodological choices, underlying modelling assumptions and scope of analysis. In this study, we present a systematic review of the studies that have examined labor impacts of energy transition to understand the underlying mechanisms that impact employment estimates. Using the Context-Interventions-Mechanisms-Outcome framework, we selected 236 papers for the study. The paper identifies multiple factors that explain these variations: first, the type of assessment used in the study impacts the projected job numbers. Gross assessment (42% of studies in our sample) provide optimistic results without accounting for the potential job losses. Second, ambitious climate action scenarios in an economy leads to the increase in projected jobs. We find that 25% of studies are dependent on the scenario assumptions. Third, employment details such as employment factors, learning effects, job quality and skills determine the intensity of the job estimates. The review suggests that only 12% of the studies have included learning effects in their assessment and 15% have assessed the skill requirements for the manufacturing of renewables. Based on these limitations in the existing literature, we have developed an analytical framework that can serve as the benchmark for studying the labor impacts of energy transitions. The framework systematically identifies and highlights the importance of integrating different elements previously discussed in the labor assessment studies to avoid the over-estimation/underestimation of employment numbers.

articles.title: When evaluation certifies international excellence: A category-validity test from Brazilian graduate education
articles.authors: Guilherme D. Garcia
articles.abstract: This article examines a category-validity problem in indicator-driven research evaluation: whether the programs a national system certifies as internationally excellent in fact publish through internationally visible journal circuits. The Brazilian federal evaluation of graduate education uses CAPES scores 6 and 7 to designate programs equivalent to “international centers of excellence”, with Qualis Periódicos serving as the journal-classification instrument for the two periods analysed (2017--2020 and 2021--2024, the closing cycles of the Qualis era). I match program-reported articles by International Standard Serial Number (ISSN) to the 2024 SCImago Journal & Country Rank (SJR) database, using SJR coverage, language, and quartiles as provisional indicators of international circulation; unmatched articles remain in the denominator, since non-indexed output is part of the policy-relevant outcome. Linguistics/Literature serves as a critical case: a field with rich local research objects, many international publication outlets, low publication-cost barriers, and CAPES 7 ratings. Across both periods the certified-excellent stratum publishes a much smaller share of articles in English, appears far less often in SJR-indexed journals, and has a very low proportion of articles in Q1/Q2 quartiles when all journal articles are counted. The case illustrates how an indicator-driven evaluation regime can sustain a stable category of certified international excellence whose alignment with externally measurable publication circuits is weak, raising broader questions about category validity in evaluation regimes for non-anglophone systems.

articles.title: Material, Epistemic, and Normative Institutional Orientations: A Common Vocabulary for Composing Social Theory
articles.authors: Michelle Anonymous
articles.abstract: Integrating fragmented social theories requires a common vocabulary that is comprehensive, generatively irreducible, persistent, and configurable, so that theories can be mapped without distortion and composed across frameworks. This paper identifies Material (M), Epistemic (E), and Normative (N) institutional orientations as a triad that satisfy these requirements. These orientations arise through the coordination of actions motivated by actor-level drives, while remaining distinct from those drives. This paper develops configurational space and locates major types of social theory as projections of that space. A worked example connects Streeck’s deferral devices to Habermas’s instrumental rationality, demonstrating the framework’s compositional payoff.

articles.title: Towards Robot Armies? On the Strategic Implications of Unmanned Ground Vehicles
articles.authors: Zachary Kallenborn
articles.abstract: Global militaries are increasingly fielding unmanned ground vehicles, but significant technical challenges continue to hinder widespread adoption. No study appears to have focused on the implications of UGVs for the strategic level of war for the United States military. This article first uses open-source research and qualitative reasoning to explore the key advantages and limitations with UGVs, then explores several areas where UGVs could have effects on the strategic level of war: supporting a new way of war, massed defense and deterrence, allied support, and low-commitment engagement and escalation. Overall, the article offers insights into how UGVs may impact military and security affairs beyond their narrow tactical use in combat.

articles.title: When Are Democracies Under Strain? Supranational Economic Integration, Financial Crises, and Satisfaction with Democracy
articles.authors: Rubén Ruiz-Rufino
articles.abstract: Why does external financial support erode democratic satisfaction in some countries but leave it intact in others? This article argues that the answer lies in the depth of supranational economic integration. Where integration is limited, conditionality releases information about government performance: elections retain their accountability function and democratic satisfaction remains stable or recovers. Where integration is deep, conditionality releases systemic information: citizens learn that elections are uninformative about future policy direction, and satisfaction falls. This integration gradient hypothesis predicts that the sign, magnitude, and mechanism of conditionality's democratic effects vary continuously with integration depth. Across five cases spanning the continuum --- Colombia and South Korea at the low-integration pole, Hungary at an intermediate position, and the Eurozone and Portugal at the high-integration pole --- the evidence is consistent with the gradient. What appears as contradictory evidence in the literature is the theoretically predicted pattern of a single mechanism at different integration positions.

articles.title: Unexpected Journeys: Russian Migrants Navigating Education and Social Spaces in the European Union
articles.authors: Mariia Daletskaia
articles.abstract: This study aims to identify how recent Russian migrant families navigate the European social space and conceptualize their newly acquired social position. It investigates the educational strategies and social integration of recent Russian middle-class migrant families within the European Union. Utilizing Bourdieu’s theoretical framework of social space and capital, the research explores how these families navigate their new social environments and conceptualize their social positions post-migration. For this qualitative analysis, data collection was conducted using semi-structured in-depth interviews as the primary research technique. The data was then thoroughly processed and analyzed using the tools proposed by Laclau and Mouffe’s discourse theory. The findings reveal that these families were among the select few in the high-income strata in Russia and now experience downward mobility upon relocating to the social space of European countries. Though this group of migrants cannot be fully conceptualized as the Global Middle Class's representatives, their actions align with the aspiration to sustain and elevate their social position. Their incomes may remain constant or even increase, yet they transition from select groups to the European middle class. Although this appears to be downward mobility, it is a strategic move to reinforce the family’s social standing within the global social space.

articles.title: From crime survey items to measurement: Developing the perceived (un)safety scale
articles.authors: Jeanette Melin; Magnus Johansson
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This study examines the ability of a new collection of survey items, the perceived (un)safety scale, to function as a coherent invariant scale. Its secondary aim is to investigate how the perceived (un)safety scale can be used to identify associations with perceived unsafety across groups.
Methods: Employing a cross-sectional psychometric design, data were collected through a postal survey in four Swedish municipal districts, differentiated by size and sociodemographic composition (n = 1,387), and a nationwide panel sample (n = 1,340). With the intention of measuring avoidance behaviours and detours due to fear of crime, the preliminary scale comprised five items. Rasch analysis was used to evaluate these measurements, and regression analyses were conducted to examine associations with individual characteristics.
Results: Initial analyses identified one misfitting item and local dependency between two items. After removing the misfitting item and combining the locally dependent items into a testlet, a unidimensional and invariant scale was obtained. Higher levels of perceived (un)safety were associated with being a woman, being younger, and having a history of victimization.
Conclusions: The perceived (un)safety scale provides a coherent and invariant measure of perceived (un)safety across demographic groups. The scale may be useful for future research, population surveys, and evaluations of interventions aimed at improving safety and reducing fear of crime.

articles.title: When Central Banks Go Green: Public Opinion and Monetary Policy Legitimacy
articles.authors: Björn Bremer; Jeffrey Chwieroth; Anita Mancosu
articles.abstract:
Climate change presents unelected central banks with an acute dilemma: acting on
climate change risks charges of mandate overreach, while failing to act risks charges
of institutional failure. Yet public opinion on green central banking remains un-
studied. We address this gap with two survey experiments in Germany and the
Netherlands. A conjoint experiment shows that adding environmental condition-
ality to corporate bond purchases significantly increases support for quantitative
easing, suggesting that greening can rehabilitate contested unconventional policies.
A framing experiment reveals that institutional objections about price stability
and democratic legitimacy erode support more than distributive objections about
job losses or asset devaluation, inverting expectations from the climate politics
literature. Respondents who trust the central bank most are paradoxically most
responsive to arguments for and against it. Public trust in delegated institutions
is thus not a blank check; it is a license granted on terms, policed most attentively
by the institution’s own supporters.

articles.title: Safeguards, Strategic Behavior, and Great Power Competition: The IAEA’s Board of Governors as an Instrument of Leverage for Potential Non- Compliers
articles.authors: Ralph Rotte; Victoria Alberty; Andreas Dürholt; René Geiser
articles.abstract:
This paper takes a critical view of the prospective ability of the IAEA to be an essential contributor to a stable
international nuclear order and prevention of nuclear proliferation, given that it is an international governmental
organization. The Agency is considered to be characterized by the ambiguities of a more or less autonomous
bureaucratic and technocratic organization led by the Secretariat. Furthermore, it is considered an
intergovernmental arena of state actors for decision-making on the political consequences of breaking Safeguards
rules with the Boards of Governors as a quasi-upstream body of the UN Security Council. As is typical for IGOs
one can therefore expect it to ultimately be an instrument of states’ foreign policy interests which reflects the
overall situation of the international system and its prevalent power structures and conflicts. Especially in times of
power transition and a revisionist dissolution of an established international order this may lead to rivalling great
powers’ acting according to their strategic priorities and protecting states that fail to fully comply with nuclear
safeguards obligations, instead of providing for effective implementation of non-proliferation measures. As a
consequence, this instrumentalization of the IAEA policy making bodies by leading powers’ strategic interests
might enable unreliable countries to avoid diplomatic pressure or sanctions for clandestine cheating or even to
whitewash their nuclear programs. By looking at the cases of Iran, South Korea, Egypt and Libya, we find that
alliance politics and strategic behavior may indeed hamper the effectiveness of the IAEA as the global nuclear
watchdog. Consequently, at least from a realist and strategic studies perspective, the IAEA and the nuclear nonproliferation
regime face an ever-increasing structural challenge in the current context of aggravating great power
competition.

articles.title: Harvesting Employment: An Economic Analysis of Odisha’s ₹3,100 Paddy MSP, Rural Youth Livelihoods, and Reverse Migration Dynamics
articles.authors: Dr Sadasiba Tripathy
articles.abstract: Odisha’s announcement of procuring paddy at ₹3,100 per quintal under the Samrudha Krushak Yojana is a notable state level intervention in terms of price support for agriculture. The central miscall of the key paddy minimum support price of the state input assistance policy is therefore expandable to beyond farm-gate price realization. This paper studies whether a higher procurement-linked paddy price can bolster rural youth livelihoods, induce seasonal labour demand, and create conditions for partial reverse migration in Odisha. The paper examines a wide range of verified secondary evidence on paddy MSP, state policy on procurement, PLFS labour indicators, MGNREGA person-days, and trend in paddy procurement in Odisha. The econometric component makes use of a clearly labelled illustrative district-level dataset for all 30 districts of Odisha since complete district-level public data linking youth employment and reverse migration is not available. Through the application of descriptive statistics, growth-rate analysis, correlation analysis and OLS regressions, we estimate the associations with agricultural procurement intensity, rural wages, availability of MGNREGA, irrigation, youth employment and potential for reverse migration. The results indicate that procurement-intense districts have better rural livelihood indicators and more reverse migration potential, but this effect is contingent on irrigation, transparent procurement, buffer stocks, milling capacity and non-farm value chain employment. The ₹3,100 paddy procurement can give a fillip to rural employment and help in migrant reintegration but only when it comes with efficiency in procurement, crop diversification, development of rural enterprises, and skills formation directed to youth.

articles.title: Digital Customer Service Adoption Barriers in Telecommunications: Evidence from a 2019 Arab Gulf Empirical Study
articles.authors: Belal A. Almomani
articles.abstract: Digital customer service has become an important component of telecommunications transformation. However, the availability of digital channels does not automatically lead to frequent or sustained customer adoption. This paper develops an unpublished MSc Business and Management research project completed in 2019 into an applied research paper on digital customer service adoption barriers, focusing on a major telecommunications operator in the Arab Gulf, which remains anonymized for confidentiality reasons. The study used a quantitative survey design and collected 271 valid customer responses. The findings showed that digital channel adoption was still developing: 41.0% of respondents used digital channels frequently, 43.5% used them sometimes, and 15.5% had never used them. The main barriers were linked to limited awareness of digital channel benefits, incomplete availability of required functions, slow request completion, complexity of use, preference for human interaction, trust concerns, and cases where digital interactions did not fully resolve customer needs. The paper positions the 2019 study as an empirical baseline for understanding digital customer service adoption barriers during an important period of telecommunications digitalization in the Arab Gulf. It argues that improving digital adoption requires more than expanding the number of digital channels. Effective adoption depends on awareness, functional completeness, speed, trust, usability, service quality, and successful service completion. The findings are discussed at a sector level, with contextual relevance to the digital transformation direction that emerged in Saudi Arabia and the wider region following the launch of Vision 2030.

articles.title: Fragmented Identity, Saffron Strategy: Navigating the Bharatiya Janata Party's Ascendance in Bodoland Territorial Region (BTR) of Assam
articles.authors: Bikash Dihingia; Chuchengfa Gogoi; Pankaj Kumar Sarmah
articles.abstract: The unprecedented rise of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the 2020 election to the Bodoland Territorial Region (BTR), erstwhile Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) of Assam, marked a significant development in the region's political landscape, which is historically dominated by the Bodoland People’s Front (BPF), an ethnic political party representing the Bodos. For decades, the BPF exercised near-hegemonic control over the BTC, shaping governance structures and political dialogue through an ethnic-centric approach. The fourth BTR election disrupted this established order and brought in a more competitive and pluralistic political environment. The shift from single-party dominance to an emerging multi-party system not only reconfigured electoral alignments but also contested the institutional and ideological bases of BPF’s authority. This study thoroughly examines the growing dynamics of electoral politics in the BTR, positioning the 2020 election as a decisive departure from conventional patterns of political mobilisation and voter behaviour. It also explores how changing socio-political conditions, including internal differentiations within the Bodo community, generated new opportunities for political contestation. Particular attention is given to the BJP’s strategic interventions, especially its capacity to leverage fragmented ethnic identities and integrate them within a wider electoral framework. Through this analysis, the study intends to advance understanding of shifting political narratives, party competition, and identity negotiations in contemporary Bodoland.
